FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Perhaps the house will permit me to present the first report of the committee which was appointed to consider the procedure of the house. I might say that the committee has come to an agreement on a recommendation to be made to the house with respect to the hours of sitting. The recommendation is that the hours of sitting should be from 2.30 to six o'clock in the afternoon and from eight to ten at night, from Monday to Friday inclusive, with the usual recess on Wednesday nights.
It is also recommended that the hour for private and public bills should be from five to six o'clock on Tuesdays and Fridays. In making these two recommendations it is suggested that the standing orders be changed to that effect. There is a further recommendation, and in this case it is not suggested that the standing order should be changed, that if the debate on the speech from the throne is not concluded after approximately the end of the first week of the session, the house should consider having morning sittings until the debate on the speech from the throne is finished.
I should also say that the committee has not given up hope entirely of reaching agreement on other matters which it has considered, and accordingly the committee recommends that it be reappointed at the next session. Under the circumstances probably it will not be necessary for me to read the report.

maintopic: FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
speechtext: Dispense.

I do not foresee that such a situation is apt to arise but it is a possibility at this time, and I think it would be prudent to have parliament in being so that it could be called by Your Honour if it should happen that there are important developments which require immediate consideration by parliament.
I should not like the public to get the impression, from the fact that there is to be an adjournment, that members of parliament consider the situation to be graver than it really is. I think the public will understand that there have been some important developments in quite recent days and that there might be other important developments of such a character as to warrant their early consideration by parliament. In that event it would be convenient to have the situation such that Your Honour could give the proper notice and have parliament assembled.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT UNTIL NOVEMBER 20, 1952, ON COMPLETION OF CURRENT BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must confess some measure of surprise at the explanation which has been given. I had not previously heard any explanation for this motion that is now before us. It has not been discussed with me nor has there been any intimation of any reason for an adjournment of parliament rather than the customary prorogation. The Prime Minister places the reason for an adjournment of this kind entirely upon the international situation. I am not aware of any events that have occurred within recent days or weeks which suggest any change in the international situation which would indicate any reason for this house to be continuing its session. I have indicated, as have other members of this party, our objection to these adjourned sessions and second sessions in the same year instead of prorogation in the ordinary way.
I would add another reason why I do not see any necessity for this motion. The house can be brought together no more quickly when it is adjourned under a motion of this

Business of the House
kind than it could be brought together if it were prorogued and then called together in a special session. If there is in fact no definite purpose in adjourning this house until November 20, then we should prorogue in the ordinary way. If there is some reason other than that indicated, then that reason should be given to us. There may be other reasons which would suggest the desirability of an adjournment instead of prorogation. I submit, however, that at any time when the world situation suggested the desirability of bringing this house together, the time within which the house could be called together would be precisely the same, whether we adjourn or prorogue.
If we have prorogued, then it is only a question of ascertaining the length of time within which hon. members, with the means of communication available to them, can come here to Ottawa. I had expected that some other explanation would be given than that which has been placed before us. The Prime Minister has been careful to say that he would not wish the public to take any alarm from the fact that he is making the suggestion that the world situation calls for an adjournment rather than a prorogation. But, Mr. Speaker, when that is the only explanation before us it is difficult to escape the suggestion that there is an intention to keep alive a sense of continuing emergency which would support the government's very clearly expressed desire to act in a great many cases under emergency legislation when they could do it very much better through legislation adopted by this house.
Either some more positive reason not yet disclosed to us should be given to us, or I submit we should prorogue in the ordinary way. The practice that has developed of adjournments for indefinite periods to indefinite dates is not a practice which we should continue at this time without something more definite than has been placed before us.

subtopic: ADJOURNMENT UNTIL NOVEMBER 20, 1952, ON COMPLETION OF CURRENT BUSINESS

am going to support the motion of the Prime Minister, because I believe that it is a wise provision for the house to make at this time. During the war years, and in times of emergency it has been customary to adjourn rather than prorogue. And while I agree with the Prime Minister that the public should not take any undue alarm at this time regarding the international situation, the recent unilateral decision of the United States to bomb the power plants on the Yalu river has I think in the minds of everyone made it obvious that there is a grave possibility in regard to it. And then of course we have the difficulties in Europe and particularly what

has happened in connection with the Swedish planes quite recently. I think under the circumstances it is a wise provision.
Moreover, it meets the objection that has been raised from time to time by hon. members of this house, the leader of the opposition, and indeed myself last year, that the calling of special sessions twice in a year means the payment of an additional indemnity. This avoids that completely. If it is necessary to call the house together, we are called together as an adjourned house. The other reason that I have in mind for supporting this is that after all in an emergency we want to meet and do business quickly. If we prorogue, then a new session is called. There are certain formalities, the official opening of the house, the debate on the speech from the throne, and so on. In my opinion, in the present circumstances, the motion to adjourn rather than to prorogue is the proper one to make at this time, and I am supporting it.

This motion proposes that the house stand adjourned until November 20 next, unless called to meet earlier under the circumstances indicated. How did this date in November come to be chosen? I am sure the Prime Minister is not unmindful of the effect that this has on all members of the house in all parties, and in fairness to the private members I would urge that this matter should have more consideration than is possible at the moment, and that the Prime Minister be asked to give very serious consideration to advancing this date from November till January. That will not subtract anything from the right of the Speaker, in consultation with the government, to call the house together at any time if emergent conditions warrant it, but I think it would be a useful contribution towards some attempt at restoration of normalcy in connection with the commencement of sessions of parliament.

subtopic: INSURANCE BOOKS FOR STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. Hodgson) asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) whether it is compulsory for students to have unemployment insurance books, and if not, what is the procedure?
The answer is that a full-time enrolled student of a day school, college or university is not insurable while he is employed (a) in temporary employment during the period from December 13 to December 31, both dates inclusive, in any year; Cb) part-time employment not exceeding 24 hours a week in the aggregate.
A student, therefore, who works after school hours or on Saturdays, so that the total number of hours worked does not exceed 24 in a week, as a general rule is not insurable. Such student is insurable if he takes full-time employment-for example during summer vacation. However if his only employment then is in a seasonal industry, for example a summer hotel, he may apply for a voluntary exemption.

Forest Conservation

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many hon. members will recall that parliament in 1947 passed the Eastern Rocky Mountain Forest Conservation Act. This act approved and ratified an agreement entered into between the government of Canada and the government of the province of Alberta for the conservation of the forests on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains. The area covers the head waters of the North and South Saskatchewan rivers and comprises 5 >
million acres, or 8,618-74 square miles. For purposes of comparison, the area of Prince Edward Island is 2,184 square miles and the area of Nova Scotia is 21,068 square miles.
The federal government's interest stemmed largely from the fact that the rivers rising in this area flow across all three western provinces and contribute in important measure to the life of western Canada and thus of the nation before they empty into Hudson bay.
This is the largest single forest conservation project in Canada and one of the largest on this continent. By protecting and conserving the forest cover in this area the two governments are providing a measure of automatic control over the flow of the rivers and streams. They are achieving soil conservation, fish and game conservation, and are ensuring sustained yield from valuable forests which are returning increasing revenues with each succeeding year.
The agreement commenced on April 1, 1948, and will continue for a term of 25 years from that date. It provides for the setting up of a board of three members, two being appointed by the federal government and one by the provincial government. The present members of the board are: Major General Howard Kennedy, chairman; G. Tunstell, Department of Resources and Development; and H. G. Jensen, province of Alberta.
The purpose and function of the board are to plan, advise, direct, and supervise the construction, operation, and maintenance of all projects and other facilities necessary for the proper protection of the forests in the area. The agreement provides for a six-year program of capital expenditures by the federal government, amounting to $6,300,000, and a maintenance program shared by the two governments, to cost not less than $250,000 and not more than $300,000 annually.
The provincial government, under the terms of the agreement, shares in the cost of the yearly maintenance program, and pays the salary and expenses of its member of the board.

The government of Canada pays the whole cost of the capital program as formulated by the board and is obliged to pay up to $175,000 yearly toward the annual maintenance costs. In addition, it of course pays the salary and expenses of its members of the board. The formula with respect to maintenance costs provides that revenues from the surface rights be available to the provincial government and that the federal government contribution for this purpose be reduced by the amount by which these revenues exceed $125,000 per annum. During the past four years, ending March 31, 1952, the total expenditures for maintenance were $1,118,196. Of this amount, Canada contributed $276,086; the balance of $842,110 was paid by the province. This amount accrued to the province in the form of revenues.
As I indicated before, the board commenced to operate on April 1, 1948, and the fourth year under the agreement ended on March 31, 1952. Approximately two-thirds, $3,849,269, of the capital program has been completed. The capital program consists of the construction of roads and trails, fire towers, buildings such as wardens' cabins and storehouses, the installation of a radio communication network and the carrying out of forest inventory surveys and other necessary investigations. As a matter of interest, I might mention that to date 147 miles of trunk roads, 140 miles of secondary roads and 257 miles of truck fire trails have been built.
There still remains to be spent on the capital program $2,450,731 and under the present agreement this must be spent by April 1, 1954. The board has requested, and the two governments have agreed, subject to the approval of parliament and the Alberta legislature, to an extension for one year of the time for completing this work. It is considered that the money could be spent to better advantage if the period were thus extended. The federal government's commitment, however, remains at $6,300,000.
On the basis of experience gained during the first four years of the agreement, and in the light of increased costs, the board considers it necessary to increase the amount to be spent annually on the maintenance program in order to ensure the carrying out of proper protection and conservation services. The agreement now limits the yearly maintenance program to a maximum of $300,000. It has been agreed to increase this maximum to $450,000 and the provincial government has undertaken to pay all the costs of the yearly maintenance program, commencing April 1, 1952.

Whereas the board now consists of two federal appointees and one provincial appointee, the Alberta government has recommended that upon completion of the capital expenditure program, that is, the date of April 1, 1955, as provided for in the agreement, which is before hon. members at the present time for approval, the composition of the board should be one federal and two provincial government appointees for the balance of the 25-year period of the original agreement. As by that time the federal government will have discharged its responsibilities for the capital program and the provincial government will have assumed the responsibility for the cost of the annual maintenance program, the recommendation seemed to me to be reasonable and it has been incorporated into the agreement before hon. members now.
I should point out, however, that there will be no change with respect to the obligation of the board to formulate programs for the yearly maintenance of a complete protective forest management service nor with respect to the obligation of the provincial government to carry out any such program for the remaining eighteen years of the agreement.
The agreement embodying the above changes has been signed by the two governments but is subject to approval by parliament and by the legislature of Alberta. The purpose of this bill is to seek parliament's approval of the agreement and to amend certain sections of the act in order that it may conform to the amended agreement.

As one

I was gratified when the bill was brought in. I understand it was first passed by the Senate, and it is now placed before us for second reading. I was also gratified with the report of the progress of the board set up under the act that was given to us just a short while ago by the minister. I think most commendable progress has been made not only in the field of capital construction but also in extending a network of roads and trails, the building of lookouts and preparation for the fighting of fire in almost every section now of that great reserve.
I was interested in this project, Mr. Speaker, from the first experience that I had in the provincial government of Alberta. It took us something like seven or eight years of rather intensive work finally to be able to get the federal government to join in an agreement such as is now embodied in the act, and I was exceedingly well pleased when we finally did get the federal government to realize that there was some federal responsibility there.
I was interested in what the hon. member for York West had to say a moment ago and the questions he asked. He asked whether this bill would be considered a prototype or pattern of future arrangements as between the provinces and the dominion in this field of forest management.
It so happens, Mr. Speaker, that the east slope of the Rockies is the watershed that feeds several very important rivers that flow across a number of provinces. The North Saskatchewan is perhaps the most important of them, although the South Saskatchewan also has its headwaters in this area. These

Forest Conservation
waters are of tremendous importance not only to the province of Alberta but to Saskatchewan and Manitoba. We in Alberta have been conscious for a good many years of the importance of utilizing the waters for irrigation purposes to reclaim many areas of dry land in our province and to bring them back into something like good production. In the course of utilizing these waters we came face to face with the necessity, however, of making some arrangement so that the sister provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba could also have part of these waters. The fact that they rose in Alberta and flowed across our territory did not give us the right to all of the water in the rivers. We realized that if Saskatchewan, for example, much of which is in the Palliser triangle, were ever to become stabilized in its agriculture, it would have to utilize this water, and there would have to be a fair division worked out.
Something the minister did not say this morning, when making his short introductory report, was that when the final agreement which was embodied in the act to set up the eastern Rocky mountains forest conservation board was made, and when the agreement was signed between the provinces, it embodied also an agreement for the division of the waters. This board has the right to allocate certain of the waters of the North Saskatchewan river and its tributaries to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I understand that allocation has been made, and that is where the federal government enters the picture-that is, chiefly as a federal party concerned with a matter which does touch the interests of more than one province.
And so the federal government did make an agreement which, I suppose, will be the prototype or pattern for years ahead, if similar situations do arise. I know of none at the moment, but there may be others in other parts of Canada. I would like to impress upon the house that the federal government, and very wisely in my opinion, did assume its part of the responsibility for preserving the watershed on the east slope of the Rockies. Otherwise perhaps there would not be waters for Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and perhaps not even for Alberta.
The area known as the east slope of the Rockies is a large one. For many years, in certain parts it has been almost inaccessible. For a province with the resources Alberta had, in the past at any rate, successfully to preserve that watershed was just more than could be expected of it. The costs were terrific. Even during the early years of my experience in the government of Alberta, fires were frequent, and at times it would cost us as much as a million dollars in a year to fight fires. That was a terrific drain on

our limited resources, and was one of the things which urged us to try to get federal help. I think all hon. members realize the federal government does have some responsibility to help a province, especially in a case of this kind in which are involved waters that flow through more than one province, and touch the interests of all those provinces very closely.
I was never quite satisfied that the federal government took its full responsibility. I do not believe the amount of money agreed to, either for capital consumption costs or for yearly maintenance, was equitably divided. I believe that right from the start Alberta has borne a bigger share of that responsibility than it should have borne, with the limited resources it had.
However, we are grateful that the agreement was made and that the federal government realized its responsibilities. I wish the minister to know that I am not criticizing anything that has been done when I say, as I do say, that the province has carried a disproportionate share of the cost of the preservation of the watershed, in view of the importance of that watershed to other parts of Canada.

As a farmer coming from a province which depends for its income almost entirely on agriculture and fishing, I

feel obligated to make a few remarks on this item. There are a few general observations I should like to make, and then I have one or two questions to which I should like answers if the minister would be kind enough to keep them in mind. It was not my intention to refer at all to the question of foot-and-mouth disease, although I did have the interesting experience of serving on the committee investigating the outbreak of that disease in Canada. It was not my intention to mention it in these remarks, but because of some of the arguments which were advanced yesterday I feel compelled to make a few observations in that regard.
I feel that, in the report of this committee, an attempt has been made to leave the impression that everything that could be done was done in an effort to stamp out the foot-and-mouth disease in this country. I think that it is admitted by everyone that, once the disease was diagnosed and identified, an excellent job has been done by those concerned in stamping it out after the middle of February; and I think they deserve the congratulations and the thanks of the Canadian people for the fine effort they have made.
When it comes to the question of the time required to identify the disease, however, I think there is a great deal of room for improvement. If the impression is left that a time lapse of two and a half months is sort of normal, or at least is acceptable, or that it even can be tolerated as a reasonable time lapse in the diagnosis of foot-and-mouth disease, I think we are doing our future cattle industry a great injustice. After all, if we hope to re-establish the confidence of the people of the United States and of the United States government-and after all, that is what we are primarily concerned with in our policy to control the foot-and-mouth disease

we must convince them that we will not leave any stone unturned in our efforts to diagnose, in as short a time as possible, any future outbreak of the disease; that we will make every effort to stamp it out; and that we will press forward towards the objective of stamping it out completely, letting the chips fall where they may, if there is any indication that there has been inefficiency on the part of anyone concerned.
Further, I think the suggestion that almost a quarter of a year is a normal time for the Canadian veterinary profession as such to require to identify foot-and-mouth disease is an unjustifiable reflection upon the profession in this country. I feel that the vast majority of men in the veterinary profession in this country, if another outbreak should occur, would be capable of having it identified in
Supply-Agriculture
an extremely short time. In the United Kingdom the experience has been that fresh outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease are not identified in a matter of months, weeks or even days but quite frequently within hours of the outbreak being recorded. The matter of time and the urgency of identifying the disease are recognized to be so highly important in the United Kingdom that, according to my information, the department of agriculture in the United Kingdom keeps a man on duty twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, for the express purpose of receiving reports of outbreaks in the United Kingdom of diseases that could possibly be foot-and-mouth disease, so that the proper authorities can be immediately alerted and the proper action can be taken at once to identify the disease and to determine whether or not it is foot-and-mouth disease.
I am convinced that the best method for us to adopt in our endeavours to regain the confidence of the United States government or the United States department of agriculture is to show a willingness to do everything possible to identify, to diagnose, and to publicize the fact of any outbreak of any disease that may occur in this country. After all, if we are to suppose that it is normal, or if we are even to suggest or to imply that it is normal to take ten weeks or so to identify foot-and-mouth disease, it is not fair to expect any country to buy cattle from us at any time if the disease may be going on in this country for ten weeks before we even know whether it is there or not. I do not think any reasonable person would expect us as a country to import cattle, sheep, or any other animal from a country which was as inefficient as that in its diagnosis of foot-and-mouth disease.

I have been disturbed by the fact that it would appear that over the last number of years the agricultural industry has been taking a less important place in our economy than it has in the past. I am disturbed by a report dated Ottawa, June 24, which points out that the farm population of this country has declined over the last ten years from
3,100,000	persons to 2,900,000 persons. That is a drop of 200,000 farm people in a ten-year period. I know, and I think it is generally recognized, that part of that drop is owing to the fact that-because of mechanization and other means which make agriculture more efficient from a labour point of view- a smaller number of people can cultivate a larger amount of land than was the case in the past. I am disturbed to notice that, in eastern Canada, not only has the farm population gone down over the last ten years but also the acreage under cultivation. That statement applies to nearly all of the eastern provinces of Canada. I think that is an extremely unfortunate state of affairs. Our agricultural industry has not only been decreasing in importance in relation to our general economy but it has been factually decreasing in importance over the last number of years. In that regard, I happened to notice that the net farm income for 1949- that is the latest figure I have-was something like $1-5 billion. The budget for last year is over $4 billion. That means that the total farm income for 1949 is only slightly more than one-third of the federal taxes which must be paid in this coming year. In other words, the federal government has become a business which is almost three times as important as one of our leading industries, namely the agricultural industry. I think that everything possible should be done to stimulate our agriculture and our industry generally, and to find markets for any products which we may have over and above those required for the consumption of the Canadian people. After all, the world population is increasing at a very rapid rate. Taking the world as a whole, our food supply, relative to our population, is becoming less and less and I believe that both from a general economic point of view, and from the

point of view of defence, everything possible should be done to bring our agricultural industry as near its potential as possible.
People will say that that is being done and that we have an excellent record as an agricultural country. We look upon ourselves perhaps with regard to the production of wheat as leading the world. I should like to quote just a figure or two with regard to that. If we look at the way in which we have exploited our possibilities with regard to wheat production we find that Canada produces only about one-third as much wheat as the United States, and only about one-third as much wheat as the U.S.S.R. Our wheat production is only slightly greater than that of France, a small European country. Italy produces almost as much as the whole of Canada. It does seem to me therefore that there is a great opportunity for us to stimulate and develop our agricultural industry as much as possible.
I feel that some of the causes of the decline in our agricultural production relative to the economy of the country as a whole in the last number of years are due to the fact that many of our farmers are not as efficient as they should be. I am very strongly in support of everything that is done by the Department of Agriculture in a scientific way to try to improve agricultural methods, but I still feel there is considerable room for research in that regard. One thing I can think of at once is the fact that in this country agricultural power as applied to farm tractors and as produced in eastern Canada is almost entirely by gasoline. In Europe it is very unusual to see a gasoline tractor on the farm. Nearly all the tractors used in Europe are diesel tractors. A diesel tractor will produce twice the amount of power on a gallon of fuel as a gasoline tractor will, and in addition to that diesel fuel costs about half as much as gasoline. Therefore from the fuel cost point of view diesel power is about one-fourth as costly as gasoline power.
I know that research is done by the Department of Agriculture into the suitability of farm machinery, but I feel that that is a phase of the scientific effort of the Department of Agriculture which should be pressed forward in every possible way. I feel, too, that much of the excellent research that has been done by the officials and the scientists of the Department of Agriculture to improve the methods of agriculture in this country is not getting through sufficiently to the people who need it most. If a farmer is a good one he tends to acquire this information for himself. He goes out and gets it. It is the poor farmer who is not so apt to seek this information himself. I welcome every

possible method which may be used or expanded to bring the information and the knowledge which is available to the people who need it most.
I am very pleased to see that the year before last some films were produced by the national film board, sponsored by the Department of Agriculture. I have not the figures for the last year. I hope that policy has been continued, and I would be interested to have a brief comment from the minister telling us the program in that regard, because I feel that the importance of getting the information at hand, the knowledge which the experts have, if you like, to the average farmer is something that cannot be emphasized too much, because in this day and age farming has become a very complicated and difficult job. If the farmers are to be efficient they must have a wide knowledge of quite a varied field with regard to the chemistry of soils, the breeding of livestock and of an infinite number of things. This requires a very good general technical education, if you like, in the vocation which they are following. I believe that any effort that can be made to improve the efficiency of the average farmer in Canada and thereby make rural life more attractive and more remunerative to the average farmer will strengthen the general fabric of our country and will be highly justified.

I wish to express my own appreciation of the type of speech which the hon. member who just took his seat delivered in connection with these estimates. The criticisms made were legitimate ones, and the suggestions made were helpful. I am sure that is what every hon. member has in mind to do, in the first place, to criticize what ought to be criticized and to try to be helpful in any suggestion made.
I should like to say, with regard to the criticism that agricultural population has been dropping in Canada during the last ten years, that there is an explanation for the figures which appear in the census of 1951 as compared with 1941, which is not apparent unless one goes into the details. The definition of "farmer" has been changed in 1951 as compared with 1941. The provision in the census of 1951 is that we do not list anyone as a farmer who is operating less than three acres, whereas in the census of 1941 we went down to one acre for farmers. Then higher incomes are required in order to say in 1951 that a man is really a farmer, as compared with 1941. That accounted for about half the difference between the farm population as listed in 1951 as compared with that of 1941.
Then I think it should be kept in mind that there was quite a change brought about by the fact that the war came in 1939, and that it developed to greater intensity in 1940 and 1941. It was widely stated during the period of the war-and I think it was generally correct-that there were about
400,000	young people on the farms across Canada in the later thirties and the early forties who under ordinary circumstances would not have been there at all. We had been passing through a very difficult economic period. Young people who had intended

Supply-Agriculture
to go to universities were not able to go. Other young people who intended to go into other employment were not able to find that employment, and they were on the farms.
Shortly after war began-at least, within two years after it began-there were 400,000 less young people on the farms, and we were producing more without that 400,000 than we had produced with them. This simply meant that following the ten years of depression there was a considerable proportion of our population who were on the farms but who did not wish to be there and were awaiting an opportunity to leave. A family of a certain size has one, two or three who must leave that particular farm and go somewhere else. That population to the extent of some
400,000	did go away, and not all of them came back, naturally.
So the farm population, as compared with 1941, is down somewhat on that account. But at the same time there is the other reason given by the hon. member for the decrease in farm population, namely that farms are more mechanized now than they were before. I think in that connection one should keep in mind the fact that while a very considerable part of the population of Canada is not now listed as farm or, in some instances, even as rural population, and while it is correct to say that, in a sense, there are between two and three million people listed as farmers, about six and a half million of the Canadian population, or almost half of it, is listed as rural. There is not a great deal of difference between a farmer and a rural person who lives in a hamlet or small town. These people live very close to the farms, and usually they are doing those things which at one time in our development were actually done on the farms. I am sure every member in the committee can remember far enough back to recall the days when a very large percentage of our hogs were actually killed on the farms and then peddled in the towns and cities. One can remember, too, back in the earlier period, when a very considerable portion of the blacksmithing and all that sort of thing was done by the farmers themselves. Eventually we had blacksmiths in our towns and villages who did that work. These people were doing work which previously had been done on the farms.
Then, as we have mechanized our farms, a great many with a mechanical turn of mind have gone to the cities and towns to produce the machinery that is needed, to repair it, and all that kind of thing. If we make allowance for that development over the years, including the development in transportation facilities and everything else that takes people away from the farms but still keeps
(Mr. Gardiner.]
them in touch with the actual production and marketing of food, and making it available to people who will consume it, we can quite easily show that a very considerable part of the six million people who are listed as rural people, together with a very considerable number of those who are even in some of our cities and towns that have been incorporated, and have therefore become urban, could compare favourably with those who had been listed previously as farmers.
In other words I think it is correct for those of us who live on farms to maintain that about half the population of Canada is really very closely associated with what we believe to be Canada's most important industry. Indeed they are so closely associated that we had 750 representatives of that group of people appear as guests of the Department of Agriculture at the Chateau Laurier the other evening. The whole 750 were representative of what might be called the secondary group of agriculturists, those who do not live on the farms but whose work is connected with that of the farms.
At the time the census was being compiled this last time I put forth a little effort to try to convince those who were making it that we should find some way of bringing those people into closer touch with our farm population in that census, in order to emphasize the fact that this country still is largely an agricultural country. I hope that by the time we get around to making another census, whatever government is here at that time will give some attention to this matter and try to indicate in the census that relationship which, I think, will give a better understanding outside this country of our position as agriculturists.	-
Then on the matter of increased production of farm products: I quite agree that, so far as we can find markets for farm products, we should encourage an increase in their production. I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member from Prince Edward Island, the most completely agricultural province in Canada; and I appreciate them as one who comes from the province which stands second to Prince Edward Island as being the most completely agricultural.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the value in our Canadian economy of the experimental farm service. As the minister indicated a moment ago, agriculture is our most important industry; and I feel that if we are to compete in world markets farming operations must be carried on on a scientific basis, and the best available farming methods ought to be used. This is especially true in western Canada, from which I come.

The three prairie provinces are essentially agricultural in nature, and because of their distance from markets and the fact that we must depend upon export trade it is essential that the costs of production be cut down as much as possible. For this reason one cannot overestimate the value of experimental farms. Therefore the expenditures the government make are, I believe, a great investment for the benefit of agriculture in this country.
Apart from the value of these experimental farms from the standpoint of making experiments, I believe the greatest value must be placed upon the educational facilities these farms offer to people in and around the communities in which they are located. Farmers have the opportunity of seeing for themselves the type of work being done. The experimental farm will serve a surrounding area of about a hundred miles.
For some time now I have been making representations to the minister and some of his officials, urging the necessity of establishing a.n experimental farm in that part of northern Alberta, east of Edmonton, from which I come. Let us take the constituency of Vegreville which I have the honour to represent. It is the most densely populated rural area in western Canada. Nearly all the people there depend on agriculture, and the farmers are interested to such a degree that some of the stock breeders have received national recognition for their stock at various livestock shows. There are a number of farmers in my constituency around Spedden, Two Hills, Vilna, Andrew and Hairy Hill who have received world recognition for coarse grains at the Toronto royal fair and the Chicago world show. According to surveys made by the National Trust Company that area contains some of the most productive grain farms in western Canada.
In spite of that I have before me a report which has recently been prepared by Mr. G. E. DeLong, superintendent of the Lacombe experimental farm, on a survey he made of that area in which he has this to say in part:
Soil erosion was considered a major problem, particularly on the sandy loam soils. No trouble was experienced in 1951 but prior to that in dry years the area was considered one of the worst dust bowls in central Alberta. Weeds were considered another serious problem. Tartarian buckwheat was serious on about 75 per cent of the land; wild oats on 50 per cent; quack grass on 5 per cent and other weeds such as stinkweed, blueburr, sow thistle, Canada thistle and mustards were prevalent in certain areas.
Further on he says:
A serious soil fertility problem has developed over a period of years. The continual practice of grain growing has depleted the soil with the result that yields have dropped off rapidly in recent years.
The closest dominion experimental farm to the area about which I am talking is at
Supply-Agriculture
Lacombe, which is nearly 200 miles away. The farm at Lacombe is doing excellent work for the benefit of agriculture, but the farmers in the part of Alberta to which I am referring do not have the opportunity of visiting that farm and deriving the beneficial values which they should be able to get. As I have pointed out, I have made numerous representations to the minister and his officials concerning the need of such an experimental farm in that area. I believe the minister is sympathetic and realizes the necessity of such an establishment; but I also think some of his officials, although realizing the problem which exists, feel that it can be remedied by means of an illustration station.
I have endeavoured to make numerous inquiries regarding the value of such illustration stations and have received opinions from many people. These opinions are expressed in the words of one, William Pidruchney, district agriculturist of Vegreville, who is recognized as very highly qualified in the field of agriculture. This is what he says:
The idea of the illustration station is not a new one and we could have had one of these established many years ago if a progressive type of a fanner had been willing to undertake the proposition. In addition, I have been observing the operation of illustration stations at other centres and feel that this type of a set-up has very little to offer for the district. The majority of the farmers who enter into an agreement with the federal Department of Agriculture do not get very much financial assistance to warrant undertaking the type of program that is required by the Department of Agriculture. The illustration station set-up may have some value in certain areas of the province-
I believe it has great value.
-but in this area I feel that there is a need of an experimental station which could be operated on the same basis as those at Lethbridge, Lacombe and Beaverlodge. It does not need to be elaborate to start out with but at least have it established on the same basis and enlarge upon it in the future.
I am drawing this matter to the attention of the minister. I feel that an experimental farm is something that is necessary. It is a vital need in the area to which I have referred, and I hope the minister will give the matter the most careful consideration.

My main reason for rising at this time is to inform the Minister of Agriculture that there is some farming carried on in the province of Nova Scotia. Last February the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture came to the conclusion that their problems were being completely neglected in so far as the House of Commons is concerned, so much so that on the 5th of February they called a conference of the members of parliament from that province. I was not at the meeting, but I received a copy of their brief.

In my opinion the logical thing for them to do is send a few farmers here to represent the industry; but until they get around to doing that the coal miners and lawyers will have to do the best they can to tell their story.
In the brief I received from the secretary of their organization they made a lot of observations with respect to imports, exports, differentials in tariffs and so on about which I am not going to speak because a lot has been said on these points, and in my opinion they have been completely covered. My impression of the problem in that part of the country is a little closer to home. I have in my hand a synopsis of a story that appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of June 25 and which is based on the last census. It shows that while there has been an upswing in agricultural production to the extent of about 6 per cent in the last ten years, during that same period there has been a decline of 17 per cent in land under cultivation in the province of Nova Scotia. Apparently we are in reverse compared with the national picture.
I do not know whether the decline in acreage is occasioned by migration to urban centres or whether it is because of uneconomic factors in the industry itself. The minister would know that better than I; but the story one gets from the last census very definitely indicates a trend away from the land in that province. There are hundreds of vacant farms on which families were raised in years gone by. They were educated, moved away, and after the old people died the land was left to stand in an unproductive state. That is one story; but in ten years, while the agricultural production and the acreage under cultivation has increased by 6 per cent on a national scale, there has been a decline in land under production in the province of Nova Scotia to the extent of 17 per cent, and it looks like a continuing decline.
No doubt the minister has seen this clipping. It is very revealing according to the last census, and it gives all the figures. I am not going to waste time reading them to the minister because he has already seen them;
[Mr. GilUs.l
but that is why I say the problem is closer to home than imports, exports, tariffs and so forth. I think something has to be done in that province with regard to the utilization of land that would be productive if properly taken care of.
I would just like to leave this thought with the minister. At the present time in that part of the country there is considerable industrial development. I have in my hand a story of the development that has taken place in Newfoundland in the last four or five years. It is contained in the June 20 supplement issue of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald which carried a complete story of the industrialization of Newfoundland during the last four or five years and the trend that is expected to continue for the next four or five years. Additional production in that part of the country means there are going to be a lot more people there, and that will mean increased markets for dairy products, meats, and that kind of thing. If we do not follow up and increase our farm production to keep it in balance with industrial production it will be a bad development, in my opinion.
I think the base for any successful economy in this country, whether in a province or nationality, is an agricultural base. As I see the development in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland now, in that area the swing is toward increased industrial production with a rapid decline in agricultural production. I think I am safe in saying that at the present time 50 per cent of what is consumed in that province by way of agricultural production comes from outside. There is a steady decline in our own production, with hundreds of vacant farms throughout the province.
I would like to ask the minister whether there is a possible chance of having the P.F.R.A. legislation extended on a national basis for use wherever the opportunity presents itself in the opinion of the department. I think the P.F.R.A. legislation has done an excellent job on the prairies, but why should that legislation continue to be applicable only to the prairies? I have figures here on the administration of the two acts and they are not very large. However, the thing that impresses me in looking through the departmental administration is the large number of engineers and trained agriculturists the minister has at his disposal. I am reasonably sure it does not occupy all of the time of that highly trained technical staff to look after P.F.R.A. legislation in the prairie provinces. Is there a chance of the government extending that legislation to the provinces of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick? I can see a potential agricultural production in Nova Scotia if it is planned according to need and to match the industrial development that has taken place.

I do not think the provincial department of agriculture, though it is a good department and has excellent field workers, has the kind of men the minister has in his department administering the P.F.R.A. legislation.
In the light of the circumstances as they exist now, with plenty of land and many farms with buildings on them, I am wondering if the minister could not prevail upon his colleagues in the cabinet to extend that legislation to augment the work being done by the provincial department of agriculture, by getting some of his personnel in there with some of the technical advice and experience they have gained on the prairies, with a view to rehabilitating the agricultural industry in the province of Nova Scotia. When the minister gets around to it I would like to have his opinion on this to see if there is a possible chance. I think the answer lies there. The figures speak for themselves. What has been done in the past is all a matter of record, but I think for the future there is a good possibility in that part of the country for greater agricultural production although I can only see it achieved if we get some national assistance such as there is in the P.F.R.A. legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I represent a riding that is in the main agricultural, and I feel I should make a few observations at this time. I quite appreciate that long drawn out remarks at this time of the session are not very popular, so I will be as brief as possible.
After all, it has been said here on several occasions, even this afternoon, that agriculture is our basic industry. It is our most important industry, and last year the agricultural income in Canada was an all-time high. According to the dominion bureau of statistics Canadian farm income for 1951 reached the all-time high total of $2,825 million. That was approximately 27 per cent higher than the farm income for 1950. It is true that 1952 prospects are not so bright, I would say mainly due to the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease that we had here in Canada.
I am not going to be quite so charitable as the gentleman who just spoke; I am going to mention the matter quite briefly. No one suggests that the health of animals branch of the Department of Agriculture, or the officials, had anything to do with the introduction of foot-and-mouth disease in Canada. That is sure. I do not think anybody suggests for a moment that the officials have been at all lax in enforcing the regulations to exterminate and clean up the disease once it was properly diagnosed. I think it is generally accepted and admitted that the officials were a little slow in detecting the disease. I think that is quite true; but I would gather now
Supply-Agriculture
that the disease is pretty well exterminated, the premises are cleaned up, and the embargo on livestock going to the United States will be lifted in the very near future, or at least at some time in the not too distant future. It has often been said that if the foot-and-mouth disease had been diagnosed earlier we would not have had nearly the economic loss that we had straight across Canada. That is a hypothetical situation and nobody can say, because the disease was probably there in a mild form two months before the embargo was imposed, or probably a little more. For those two months cattle were moving quite freely, and shipments of cattle to the United States were fairly heavy. I would say that under the law of general averages, if the embargo had been placed on two months earlier it would have been lifted two months earlier. The same thing is true the other way around; if it was placed on two months later it will be lifted two months later. By and large I think it will be just about an even break.
I was amazed last night, as a matter of fact, at the exhibition we had here regarding foot-and-mouth disease, with charges and counter-charges being hurled across the house. I have often wondered if committees play as important a part as we think. It is true they have a useful function, but very often members use committees to practise up for speeches they want to make in the house, and here on many occasions we have repetitions of speeches made in committee. This happened quite frequently in the committee studying foot-and-mouth disease, and also in other committees I have attended. I have often wondered why it is regarded as so important to put all the evidence on Hansard. I have often suggested, and I am going to suggest it in the next session too, that if we could stop the franking of political speeches that are made in the house we would shorten the sessions by at least two or three months.

This adds up to approximately 8,371,000 head of cattle in Canada. By and large I think our economic loss was about the same per capita in so far as the number of cattle we had was concerned. The cattle slaughtered because of foot-and-mouth disease numbered 1,343. All those cattle did not have the disease; many had been associated with cattle who had it, or had been exposed to the disease in some way. Out of 8,371,000 head of cattle in Canada we only slaughtered 1,343. I believe that was a small percentage. I must confess, and I am quite sure most people would agree, we made a lot of fuss and created a lot of advertising about the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in this country. We hope the outbreak is over, and we think it is; and we have only lost 1,343 head. Really, we advertised it not only in this country but around the world. I think it was advertised far too much.
As I said before, the livestock producers and the people handling livestock products have had the greatest loss as a result of the foot-and-mouth disease. For instance, I am interested in egg production. The production of eggs has been quite high and the price has been comparatively low. Just as a matter of record last week a friend of mine showed me an egg grading slip which was dated April 20, 1935. It was for a small shipment of 13 dozen eggs. According to this slip the extras brought 13 cents and the first grade 11 cents, or a total of $1.52 for the 13 dozen. Taking the same quantity of eggs and the same date this year, April 20, they would have brought $4.26, so we have come a long way in that period of time. I am not saying for a minute that the price of eggs is high enough. I think it was fortunate for the egg producers that there was a floor price under eggs. March and April is the period of the highest production, and if the floor had not been established the price of eggs would have gone even lower. I would suggest to the minister and his officials that, because of the high cost of production of eggs, they revise the floor price to give the producer a fairer margin of profit. I think that is something that should be undertaken all along the line.
In the main, grain production has been fairly good and the price has been fair. Cash field crops have maintained fairly good prices throughout the year. The brightest spot we have in our southwestern Ontario crops is probably the sugar beets. I want to mention them because not many people are interested in the production of sugar beets. In this country we produce sugar beets in four provinces, Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba and Alberta. In 1951 Canada produced 241 million pounds of sugar in these beet factories. Ontario led

the field, because last year we had an exceptionally good crop. The two factories that are situated at Chatham and Wallaceburg produced 94 million pounds of sugar and processed 341,991 tons of sugar beets. The sugar content for the entire crop averaged a little over 17 per cent, which is rather exceptional. The two plants in western Ontario processed approximately 5,700 tons of beets a day. During the season they employ over 1,000 people. Last year the growers received something over $5,250,000, and a further payment is still to be made.
This year in the western Ontario district the growers have planted over 30,000 acres of sugar beets. The factories have a capacity for processing approximately 400,000 tons of beets, and it is hoped this year to attain that approximate figure, although the season has been dry and germination is very spotty. At the moment the prospects do not look very good. However, in this country we produce only about one-quarter of the sugar we consume. I often think of the tremendous progress this industry has made since the thirties, when we received only $4 or $5 a ton for sugar beets. In those times it was most difficult to keep the sugar beet industry going. At this time I want to pay tribute to my good friend the hon. member for Lethbridge, who contributed so much to the industry at that time, as well as my good friend the hon. member for Essex South. They have done a great deal to sponsor and maintain the sugar beet industry through these difficult times.
At this time when we are spending so much money on research and expansion, I should like to suggest to the minister that more money be spent on experimentation and the development of greater food crops. This is particularly true with respect to the sugar beet industry, because the sugar content of the beets has steadily increased over the years. In our district 10 per cent used to be a good average, but it has now gone up to close to 17 per cent. Great progress has been made in research at the experimental farm. I think that is the solution to our farm problems. We should grow better crops and improve our understanding how to grow them. The government can contribute a great deal-although it is contributing some, I think a great deal more could be done-in this reseach and experimental work in order to increase production in this country.
There is a special reason for dealing with one or two of these questions at this time, Mr. Chairman, as some members are going away.

I just want to raise one question, and it will only take a minute or two.

As the minister probably knows, I come from an agricultural constituency, to a great extent mixed farming; but they are chiefly interested in dairying. The producers in my constituency, like those in other parts of Canada, are greatly concerned over the dairy situation. The point I wish to bring before the minister today has to do with feed grain assistance. I understand he made some remarks with regard to that matter last night, but I was not here; I was in committee.
The point the dairy farmers in my constituency raise is the fact that there is not any permanency to this feed grain assistance. They say it is hard for them to make their plans for the future when, from year to year, they never know whether or not this assistance is to be continued. I was wondering whether the government could have some sort of permanent policy so the dairy producers in the maritime provinces would know, from season to season or from year to year, whether this assistance would be on a permanent basis. That is the point that I wish to bring before the minister.
While I am on my feet I might say that I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South in many of the remarks he has made. It is not production that is the chief problem for the farmers in the maritime provinces. As the hon. member said, we have a great many abandoned farms. Those farms are not abandoned because we cannot produce; the fact is that we could produce far more in my constituency, and the same is true with regard to most of the other constituencies in the maritime provinces. Our big problem is the question of markets.
Hear, hear. That is everybody's problem.

Until we get stable markets in this country; until we get stable markets for the farmers of the maritime provinces -and I think this is true with respect to farmers all across Canada-we shall have vacant farms and more vacant farms. I often hear it said that in my own province of New Brunswick we could have a population two or three times as large as we have, both in our towns and in our rural areas, if the products we raise on our farms could be sold at prices which would make it profitable for the farmers to raise them, and make it possible to keep the young people on the farms.
That is the only point I wish to raise at the present time. I should like to ask the minister whether it is at all possible to assure the dairy farmers of the maritime provinces of some permanency in this feed grain assistance.

Mr. Chairman, what I was going to say was that I have been agreeing to have members rise in their places and speak on individual matters which will come under votes we shall be coming to later on. I do not raise the usual objection to that kind of thing on the general discussion because I take it for granted that hon. members, as we are coming to the end of the session, are desirous of expressing themselves from time to time, and that they will probably be prepared to pass the individual items more readily when we come to them-more readily than has been the case at some other times. I am therefore not insisting that we get done discussing them generally, and get by item No. 1, and wait discussion until we reach the items.
I will review one or two matters that have been raised, with a view to mentioning some other things hon. members probably will want to give thought to, inasmuch as we are drawing toward the close of the session.
First I should like to say a word or two with regard to the suggestions made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. Since 1943 we have been considering the possibility of bringing down legislation to apply the principle of P.F.R.A. right across Canada. At that time we had a committee of the house which gave careful study to the whole question and recommended that course. On three or four different occasions since that time I have had ready bills to make that procedure a possibility. I also think that hon. members can have as much influence upon the government as I can in connection with a matter of that kind. The subjects that have come up for consideration here from session to session, and to which great importance is attached, are naturally the subjects to which hon. members of the government are giving the most attention. While we have had bills prepared from session .to session, we have had little discussion of the question. Little has been said about it. The result has been that the legislation having to do with this subject is passed over to another session. That is one suggestion I should like to make. On a practical problem of that kind, discussion would probably get us a little bit farther than the discussions we have on some other things.
I should say this with regard to the matter. There seems to be a misunderstanding with regard to what happens in the west. P.F.R.A. covers only a small part of western Canada. It covers less than one-third of the three prairies provinces. It does not cover any of British Columbia. It does not cover the northern part of any of the three prairie

Supply-Agriculture
provinces. As a matter of fact it covers a small proportion of the province of Manitoba. Those who are living in other parts of Canada should not conclude that P.F.R.A. applies to all of the western provinces. It does not. It applies only to the Palliser triangle to which reference was made last night by the hon. member for Lethbridge.
The other point I should like to make at the moment is that in the maritime provinces we have legislation covering the marshlands, and that legislation was patterned after the legislation we have in the west in connection with P.F.R.A. To the extent that we are spending money on marshlands in the eastern part of Canada, we are doing the same thing there that we are doing in a comparatively small section of western Canada. The officials who have been trained in one area are transferred to the other, back and forth, in order to assist in that work.
So far as most of the farmers in Canada are concerned-and this is true so far as I am concerned personally-I think they would like to see legislation which covers all of Canada. The legislation in the east would require to be different from that in the west. The provisions made for British Columbia would be somewhat different from those made for the prairie provinces. On the prairies our problem is entirely, or almost entirely, a drought problem, a problem of lack of moisture. In British Columbia it is both; on one side of the mountains it is a drought problem; on the other side it is one of too much water. The problem down in the eastern part of Canada is that of salt water coming in on the land. That is not helpful. The objective is to keep it out. Those are all great problems. In this department we have always had the feeling that the whole matter could be dealt with right across Canada, with one staff of engineers, to better advantage than it can be dealt with in ten provinces. Nevertheless up to ithe present time, under our constitution the responsibility is fundamentally provincial; and it is only in dealing with certain phases of it that the federal government has come into the picture.
With regard to the suggestion that there are vacant lands in the maritime provinces, I may say I am not so familiar with the vacant lands in those provinces as I am with Ontario, although my deputy who is sitting here was born and raised in Nova Scotia. I have visited the area where he was born and raised. I have visited most of the areas in Nova Scotia. I just asked my deputy about the lands where he was born, and he says that they are grassed.
They must be productive lands.

That is true of lands in western Ontario; they are grassed. That does not mean that they are not producing. As a matter of fact, grassed land upon which you are pasturing cattle, having regard to the present price of cattle, may be bringing the farmer more money than they would if he were living there and producing crops by hard labour. In other words it requires a little more labour to produce turnips, and all that kind of thing, and feed them to cattle than to grow grass and pasture the land with cattle. To the extent that is being done both in Ontario and in the maritimes the owner of the land may be taking in more money than can be acquired in any other way. I quite agree there are some arguments in favour of having other kinds of production, and I like to see an agricultural area being cultivated and producing as intensively as it possibly can produce. Whether you can have that or not depends somewhat on the further question as to how dense your population is. That density of population, of course, depends upon the development of industry and other matters, and to the extent that the population is there to consume the type of thing, vegetables and small fruits, which would grow on that intensively cultivated piece of land a market can be found. These things all go together and have something to do with the matter.
The other question which was raised had to do with experimental farms, and particularly experimental plots, illustration stations, or experimental stations in different parts of Canada, and particularly in the province of Alberta. There is an area which has been referred to by the hon. member for Vegreville, who comes from that section, which I think personally, along with the hon. member, requires some special attention. There are areas in other parts of Canada that are similarly situated. The soil is of a little different character from the soils in places where we have stations now, and the people are all pretty much of one nationality, having come here from a section of Europe which is very highly agricultural. The conditions being different from those they were accustomed to there is further reason why we should have a station of some kind there. As the hon. member has suggested, we are quite willing at any time to put in what is called an illustration station. One of the reasons for our willingness in that regard is naturally that the cost is not so high.
The suggestion is made that the illustration station is not so useful. I must say that in going across the country I have wondered sometimes whether that is true or not. In travelling across Alberta and Saskatchewan,

and even some of the eastern provinces, I have found our cereals men holding meetings at these little illustration farms, and I have been surprised at the number of people who gathered around listening to the story they were telling. Then I have gone to our experimental farms and I have been surprised at the few times I found anybody there. We have these rather large experimental stations and farms right across the country, and one just wonders sometimes why there are not more people there taking advantage of what can be learned by visiting these places.
On the other hand, when you advertise a class for a certain date at a certain illustration station and have a few of the officials from the department there to give lectures on what this means and what that means, it is surprising the number of people who turn out and examine the rows of grain and walk up and down the rows, and examine the different varieties of cereals that are being produced in those little plots. Then they go home and try to do the same thing themselves, or try to produce in the same way. I would suggest to the hon. member that there is a great deal to be said for the illustration station as a starter at least, even if you are not able to get the experimental farm that is thought to be advisable. At the same time I want to emphasize my own sympathy with the contention that he has made here this afternoon that in that particular area there should be something more than that.
There is no special vote for it in our estimates of this year. There is a general vote for illustration plots which can be enlarged upon somewhat from the small plot, and something along that line could be started this year with the idea that it could be developed into something better. But that is the general position right across the country. Take Beaverlodge, which was mentioned a few moments ago by the hon. member. The first time I went to Beaverlodge, which is up northwest of Edmonton toward the British Columbia boundary, it was just a little better than an illustration station. People were gathered there in a considerable group to listen to the lectures by officials of the department. I happened to be in that section of the country at that time, and I went there. That was probably 15 or 16 years ago now. I was back there two years ago, and I was agreeably surprised-and I emphasize the word "surprised"-to find just how much I had been able to persuade this house to pass by way of votes in order to improve and enlarge upon the plant which is there. It is now quite an important experimental farm, with very much more equipment than I expected to find when I went to visit it, and very much more in the way 55704-243i

of buildings. But I would suggest to hon. members that they not be too anxious about getting started at the top. If you cannot get started in any other way than at the bottom, then start at the bottom. Get started, and no doubt as we go along and have experience with it we will be able to do even more than is expected by some.
With respect to the production of sugar beets and other products of that kind on our farm lands, we have specialties of course right across the country, and we do co-operate in every possible way with the provinces in connection with their development. But I have followed the practice while I have been in the department-and I think it is the proper practice to follow-of relying considerably upon the provincial departments of agriculture to give the lead in the agitation for a certain use of land as compared with the use that has been made of it previously. The obvious reason for that is that after all it is the provinces that deal with these people as individual farmers. They have to do with building the roads for them; they have to do with putting in schools for them; they have to do with all the developments that are to take place there. Therefore I hesitate, as Minister of Agriculture for the dominion, to say that people ought to be growing more sugar beets some place, or they ought to be growing tobacco here and corn somewhere else. I think that lead should be given by the provinces; then we can come along and help not only in the further production but in finding markets for the products. We think that we ought to do that to the greatest extent possible.
I was very pleased to hear what has been said with regard to all these products in order that we might be in a better position to assist with them as we go along.
I have been waiting until the leader of the opposition came back to say this to him, and I want to say it now. We had a little discussion this morning about an agreement that was entered into in the early part of the session. I want to say to him that he carried out his agreement with me in every particular. There was no way in which he broke his agreement. The same is true of the leader of the C.C.F. party. The only agreement I got from the leader of the Social Credit party when I made the suggestion was that he waved his hand to me. Well, unfortunately, that does not appear in Hansard and there is no reference in Hansard to anything he said. The leader of the official opposition said that he was within reason prepared to go along and get this legislation through and, as a matter of fact,
