if you look in Hansard you will find that we jumped all the different two days' notices that we give from one step to another, and we went completely over into committee. It was in committee that we took up considerable time, but the leaders all agreed to facilitate passage. I knew the leaders did not have an opportunity between the time I was talking to them and the time we came into the house to talk to all their members, or to hold a caucus of their groups or anything of that kind and to tell them. I can understand that some individual members did not know, and that they may have taken up more time than otherwise they would have taken up. But I am simply saying now that I agree with what the leader of the opposition said this morning, that he did carry out any undertaking he gave; and that is true of the leaders of the other groups as well.
The minister did not answer the question I asked him.

On the question of feed
grain freight, I have wondered sometimes why farmers do not take it for granted that, since we have been paying the freight since 1941, we are likely to go on paying it. We are always in the position, no matter how we go about it, that we can change at any time, even if we had legislation which stated that it was continuous until further notice. That is all the legislation does say, as a matter of fact; it can be withdrawn at any time. In the manner in which we are operating now, we go on from year to year. Under the provisions we now have, the government simply say they will continue it until next year, and we pass our estimate for that purpose.
I did announce yesterday when I brought down the estimates that there was in them an amount of $11,125,000 to cover feed grains freight assistance for this year. I am not at all satisfied that I would be able to have any more than that done. The government rather feels that this is something which may require changing from time to time. I have not heard any suggestion that it ought to be cut out, but there has been a suggestion made that perhaps it should be changed.
It has not been changed materially except when freight rates have been changed; we have made some changes in order to bring it into line with changes in freight rates. However, it has gone on now for quite a few years on much the same basis, and I would imagine some special condition would have to arise to bring about a discontinuance of the payments.

There is just one matter I wish to make clear in relation to what the Minister

of Agriculture said about the agreement that was referred to on an earlier occasion. I think it is necessary to leave no uncertainty as to what the agreement was and as to what was under discussion, in view of certain earlier debate in relation to which the minister and I had some comments to make this morning.
I am very pleased that the minister has without reservation stated that I carried out any undertaking I gave. I do however think there should be more on the record than has already been told. The discussion arose because of a charge that the hon. member for Lake Centre had failed to carry out an agreement. I want to make it clear as to what the agreement was. That agreement was to permit a measure to provide for compensation to those who had lost animals as a result of foot-and-mouth disease to have priority over any other legislation.
The session was just beginning, and ordinarily we would have proceeded with other government business. I was approached and asked what my position would be in regard to the introduction of a measure which would make it possible to deal immediately with compensation. It was pointed out that the passing of such a measure would help to restore confidence among the farmers who were losing animals in this way, and also that it would encourage other farmers to report the disease as quickly as possible, if it appeared, because they would know that there was going to be some provision made for them.
Naturally I agreed immediately to that proposal. There was no undertaking as to length of debate or otherwise. Most certainly there was no suggestion that there would not be adequate discussion of the measure which came before us. Hansard will show that this important legislation was dealt with expeditiously. I do wish to say in relation to this that not only was my undertaking as leader of the Progressive Conservative party carried out, but that there was no single member of this party who in any way opposed the adoption of the legislation or who failed to carry out the spirit as well as the letter of that undertaking.

I am not going to read what took place, because it would take some time to do it; but it bears out pretty much the statement that has been made by the leader of the opposition. Hon. members will find the arrangement that was entered into clearly stated to the House of Commons at page 32 of Hansard for this session.
I am simply going to leave it there, and say that anyone who wishes to read what the

understanding was may do so. I spoke, stating what the understanding was. Then the leader of the official opposition spoke very much along the lines he has spoken today. The leader of the C.C.F. followed and stated his position. Then, as I say, my hon. friend the leader of the Social Credit party agreed by a wave of his hand, as much as to say, "Go ahead". And we proceeded from that point to do whatever was required.
I just wish to make it understood that there was some understanding; and my suggestion is that, so far as the groups as such were concerned, they carried it out.

Just to tie it in-because it has been the subject of discussion in as well as outside the house, apparently with the purpose of creating the impression that the hon. member for Lake Centre had failed to carry out an undertaking-I wish to make it abundantly clear that when we agree at any time to permit the introduction of legislation in this manner, we certainly do not agree to abandon any opportunity for debate or such discussion of a measure which is introduced as is regarded as appropriate under the circumstances.
I wish to leave no doubt as to the suggestion that the hon. member for Lake Centre in any way impeded the proceedings of the house or failed to carry out any undertaking. I repeat that the hon. member for Lake Centre and all other members of this party fully carried out any undertaking or understanding to which I had been a party.

When the legislation dealing with compensation in respect of animals was before the house, I was one of the first members to speak for this group. On that occasion, while I spoke for only a moment or two, I stated that I did not feel any good could be accomplished by prolonging the debate. I believe our actions during the sittings of the committee and since that time have indicated that we have carried out entirely the sign made by our leader, the hon. member for Peace River.

Before we leave that, and before the leader of the opposition leaves the chamber, I wish to say that I agree with what the leader of the opposition has said, and what others have said. But I am sure the leader of any of the groups would be the first to say that whatever arrangement had been made did not bind individuals. I think those of us who are also individuals in the house will have to be allowed to hold our own opinions with regard to the actions of any individual in relation to the matter. That

I agree with the hon. member who has said that if we did not have the opportunity to express our opinions, there would be no use in our coming here. When the day comes that I cannot express my opinion, I shall stay at home.
I understand the hon. member for Vegre-ville has requested the establishment of an experimental station in his constituency. While I was not in the chamber to hear what he said-I was busy attending to other matters elsewhere-I believe he has made a good suggestion. When the minister is considering it, I would ask him to consider at the same time the request made by the farmers of Derwent district, located 25 miles north of Vermilion. In all fairness to the hon. member for Lake Centre; even in spite of the fact that the Minister of Agriculture says that what was right and what was wrong has been clearly understood; also in view of the fact that I took some part in that debate, I should like to make it very clear-and it is to be found on page 32 of Hansard for March 3 if anybody wants to read it-that the leader of the opposition did not at any time consent to the passage of that bill without discussion. That was the only consent he gave. The Minister of Agriculture is leaving the impression-

This is what the leader of the opposition said:

I want to say a few words, first of all on the subject of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the question of its extension to other parts of Canada besides the three prairie provinces. I shall be brief and very general at this stage because I want to ask one or two specific questions when we come to the particular item in the estimates. However, with respect to the general aspect of the matter I think the minister will agree with me when I say that I have on a number of occasions, urged-and indeed supported the suggestion of the minister-that there be an extension of the act so that it might have general application to the whole of Canada, as he has himself suggested this afternoon.
I recall an occasion in 1947 when it was understood, or at any rate, certainly it was very strongly hoped, that legislation extending the act would be introduced. My recollection is that the proposal at that time was to have two separate bills, one extending it westward to British Columbia and another making it of application in the eastern part of Canada. I have never ceased to hold the view that the general provisions of the act
[The Deputy Chairman.]
should be extended so that instead of prairie farm rehabilitation engineers being called upon to go into our province, as at present, only when certain specific local projects arise, or only when specific requests are received from provincial authorities, they might take part, in co-operation with the provincial authorities it is true, in a general study of all problems of water conservation and land reclamation as well as irrigation which the minister has said vary so widely from area to area in our province.
I have been particularly interested in the question of a general study of the joint problems of irrigation, flood control and power development in the Fraser river system where all these three problems exist, and in the lower reaches of the Fraser where the problems of reclamation and diking exist. I have urged and still urge that, although a study is now going forward on that matter, there should be a clearer definition of the federal authority under which that study is going forward. While I have the highest admiration and respect for both the dominion and provincial officials who are taking part in the study, and while I know they are making all the progress they can with the resources at their disposal, my feeling is there could be a greater drive and sense of urgency from the top. It is my feeling that at the present time there is not that sense of urgency and push behind the thing from this level that perhaps there might be. That drive from above is one of the things which I think would result if an act were passed making the principles of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration of general application to the whole of Canada.
While I do not necessarily say I will wait until he himself brings it forward, I want to assure the minister that if at any time he does bring forward such a proposal he can count on my immediate and full support. I hope indeed that he and the government as a whole will take these remarks as an indication from me that I think this matter should be proceeded with now. My recollection is that the last time we discussed the matter on the minister's estimates he told me that it had been his intention, as I think he said today, every year since 1947 to bring in bills along the lines of those which he discussed, but I think it was in 1950 or 1951 when he told me that because of the sudden way in which defence requirements had taken priority it had been decided that, temporarily, it would not be possible to proceed with that policy. My recollection again is that he assured me in reply to a question that I was correct in assuming this was only a temporary postponement.
That is right.

I am sure we can give those words their literal interpretation. While I realize that defence requirements and the priority of defence expenditure still exist, nevertheless I hope we will not be compelled to defer too long our hope that the project can be proceeded with. If the minister is in a position at this time to give us any general outline of what the position is with respect to the relationship between defence priority and this type of project, I think it would be very helpful.
Then, Mr. Chairman, at this time I would like to ask the minister a question or two with relation to the support price policy for beef which he announced recently as a result of the closing of the United States market to our cattle. I ask these questions at this time because I have to say that my correspondence and conversations with the minister and some of his officials have not yet produced an answer to these questions satisfactory to myself or to the B.C. beef cattle growers association who have their head office in my constituency. The questions relate to the specific application of the price support program to cattle originating in British Columbia.
It has been drawn to my attention that as a result of personal interviews by the manager of one of our largest cattle ranches- as a matter of fact the largest in Canada-as a result of his personal views with the officials of the packing plants operating in the city of Vancouver he was advised they had no instructions from the department as to any support price policy for beef originating in and marketed in British Columbia. They had instructions with respect to the handling of beef marketed in British Columbia but originating in provinces other than British Columbia, but they had no instructions with regard to British Columbia beef. Indeed they indicated to this gentleman that as far as they were concerned the lack of such instructions from the department indicated that there was no support price program for beef originating in British Columbia, and so the association asked me to take this matter up and find out why that should be the case.
When I discussed it with the deputy minister and later with the minister it was indicated to me that one reason is that British Columbia is a deficiency province; that is, it does not produce all the beef which we ourselves consume, and further, that Vancouver market prices are well over the floor price which would apply under the support program and therefore there did not seem to be any practical reason why instructions should be issued at this time as to how to apply price support to British Columbia beef.

Well, Mr. Chairman, it has been indicated to me quite clearly by the B.C. beef cattle growers association that they do not regard that as a satisfactory answer. One of the reasons they are not satisfied, as pointed out by the secretary of the association in a letter to the deputy minister, a copy of which I have received, is that it has been their experience that-
. . . unless the machinery is set up beforehand there are always delays in putting a scheme like price support into effect when it is needed.
That answer relates to the statements which have been made by the departmental officials that there is no need for such instructions to be issued at this time because British Columbia prices are well above the floor. The concern of our cattlemen is that although that is true at the present time, nevertheless our cattle will be moving on to the market from the grass in increasing numbers toward the end of this month, and from then on in increasing numbers through the rest of the year. Should any surplus on the market occur as a result of the American embargo, or as a result of some difficulty developing in the four-way meat deal between Canada, the United States, New Zealand and Great Britain, then a support price would be an immediate necessity in British Columbia.
It was relating to that statement by the department and from a practical point of view that they say:
. . . we have always found that, unless the machinery is set up beforehand there are always delays in putting a scheme like price support into effect when it is needed.
Other reasons they advance as to why there should be instructions issued now to packers in British Columbia may be found in this passage of the letter from the secretary to the deputy minister:
Although marketing on the Vancouver yards has increased lately such marketing is still confined to smaller shipments and does not reflect the bulk of sales of the better cattle. These are bought at country shipping points by the packer buyers. In most cases the B.C. livestock producers' co-operative association has a salesman there to act for producers. In many ways the average of prices at these shipping points is a truer reflection of cattle prices in British Columbia than the Vancouver yards, operated by the same co-operative.
The point there, which I am sure the minister and his officials will appreciate, is that the department has been relying, in their answers to the association, on the prices quoted at the Vancouver yards. The fact is that, from now on particularly, the bulk of the buying in British Columbia, as our own cattle come on the market, will be done at the interior points of origin of the cattle and not

Supply-Agriculture
on the Vancouver market. The prices there may not necessarily be the same as Vancouver prices. Therefore unless support price instructions are issued to the packers so that their buyers will know how it operates and will clearly understand that support prices do apply in British Columbia, these packer buyers may feel free to try to buy cattle at the interior points at less than the floor price.
Then the letter goes on to say:
. . . you say that you are asking the board . . .
That is the agricultural prices support board.
... to review the question of purchase of cattle originating in B.C. This association is in full accord with the sense of that paragraph, and it is in fact the nub of our contention that when British Columbia cattle of the specified grades and weights are available they should be eligible for support board purchase; otherwise, the packers will not be interested in them. Within the next thirty days...
This letter is dated June 20.
. . . we shall be moving dry cows and heifers, many of which will come within the specifications. Most of these will be offered at country points. For this reason I trust that the board will soon accept carcasses of cattle originating in B.C. on the same basis as from other provinces.
The letter goes on to pay a compliment and I think I should read this as well:
Your department is to be congratulated on arranging the exchange plan between Canada, New Zealand, United States and Great Britain. I believe that favourable comment on this would have been made at our annual meeting had it not been that producers in this province appeared to be specifically excluded from participation.
Mr. Chairman, I hope that the minister will now say that, although it may have been the situation perhaps up to the present that prices in B.C. generally have been above the floor, nevertheless because this matter is of such great concern to our producers, and in the light of the arguments advanced by them, there is no reason why he should not issue instructions to the packers in British Columbia making it clear that beef support prices apply to beef originating in our province just as they apply to beef originating in other provinces. That should be made clear to the packers.
Before I take my seat I want to refer to one other thing mentioned this afternoon. It is the matter of experimental farms. I want to express the appreciation of the cattle growers of British Columbia, particularly in my district, for the re-establishment in the last five or six years of a range experimental station and the establishment of the experimental farm at Kamloops. What the minister said with respect to finding that a relatively small number of people go to those experimental stations for instruction on what is going on, may apply elsewhere but it has not been my impression with

respect to the establishment in Kamloops. Certainly it has been my impression that the cattle growers of our district are interested in this problem generally and are very appreciative of the good work being done by the staff of that range station and farm. If the situation which the minister outlines is of general application then I shall be very glad indeed to discuss it with the association and see if there cannot be found ways to make them aware, and to make all their members aware of what goes on there and of the value to them of actually going for consultation and visits to that farm.
I want to assure the minister that the cattle growers in my area appreciate what is done there and would not want him or any of his officials to have the impression that they regard it only as of passing interest. I know they appreciate it and I shall certainly try to see, if it is the case that there have not been many who visit and take advantage of the services available, that the situation is rectified in the future.

In view of the fact that the hon. member has raised this question, which I am sure is in the minds of a number of members, and has stated it in relation to an area which has been the last to benefit by what has developed in connection with the arrangements with Britain and New Zealand, perhaps I should deal with the matter at this time. In introducing the estimates yesterday I said that our main problem in connection with the marketing of products this year has developed from the fact that we had foot-and-mouth disease, and the adjustments that had to be made as a result of that. I believe it is quite proper to say that there would not have been any floor price under cattle or beef if it had not been for that epidemic.
The question that was being discussed all across Canada prior to that was whether we should not have a ceiling price. The consumers were very much worked up over the fact that prices were so high during 1951 and were continuing at that level in 1952. If there was any agitation for anything, it was for the control of that situation. But as soon as we had foot-and-mouth disease the price dropped. If the governments had not done anything-I take into account both provincial governments and the federal government -there is very little doubt in my mind that the price of cattle would have gone down to 15 cents or perhaps 10 cents a pound. When you throw on the market a quarter of the product which had been sold outside the country, and say there is no place it can be

sold except in this country, that can have only one result and that is to push the price down.
I have noticed some criticism, which I am sure none of the members of this house would agree with, in some articles that have been written across the country to the effect that we should have allowed that to happen. The producer had benefited so long from higher prices, the consumer should have been permitted to get the advantage of lower prices for a while. I do not believe there has been much support for that idea, either amongst the consumers or any other body of people.
The farmer was just beginning to enjoy prices which enabled him to live at a standard comparable to the rest of the country.

It was quite strongly
expressed for a short time. We took the position that we should put a floor under cattle and we should offer to buy. We set the price at 25 cents a pound for good steers, but we did not expect the price would remain at that level for any great length of time, although we did expect we might buy some at that price. We not only established the price at 25 cents; we established at different points prices we would pay for beef based upon that 25 cents. In other words there was a floor set at Winnipeg, at Regina, at Saskatoon, at Calgary, at Edmonton and at Vancouver, as well as at eastern points.
The provinces took certain actions which, for a time, made it impossible for the floor price to operate freely. When we made arrangements with Britain, New Zealand and the United States to make possible the marketing of the surplus from this country, we did make the provision that we were prepared to buy anywhere at a price for meat which would bear the proper relationship to the 25 cents for good steers. There was a period-it might have been a week or two weeks, I have not looked up the records -when we were , only buying meat from Alberta and Ontario. The fundamental reason for that was that the storages in those two places were filled to the roof. Farmers could not get their animals in at all, or when they did get them into the yard they got a much lower price than they should have received because the packers had no room in the storage plants. We took action just as fast as possible, and it was in those two markets that most of the heavy cattle were to be found. They had been prepared for the United States market. There was no considerable market in this country for that heavy beef, so we went into Alberta and Ontario and bought those heavy steers first.
Supply-Agriculture
This accounts for the fact that we set a certain weight level below which we would not buy for a time. We advised holding other weights at home.
Then when we got rid of that we expressed our willingness to buy in other places. We did n'ot buy in Manitoba until that province removed its controls. We did not buy very much in British Columbia until British Columbia took off its controls. In the press today I noted the suggestion that Quebec is now removing its controls. Well, that causes me to say that we have not forced anybody to take off controls. We took the position we were able to accomplish what we had in mind without using that legal right, which we may have had, to force people to do certain things. We went along, and eventually they have found it to advantage to come along with us, so they came along.
Now, in so far as British Columbia is concerned, I think about the time this letter was written, to which reference has been made, instructions were given to the packers in Vancouver to buy meat for delivery under the British arrangement. My understanding is that a considerable part of the product which is being killed in Vancouver now is going out through the Panama canal to Britain under that arrangement. This, of course, was expected from the beginning, and did come into operation in due course.
With regard to the buying of live animals, I may say that we have bought very few live animals. In Alberta they have a system under which they have operated for a good number of years. Under this system they have auctions throughout the province, and the farmers bring their cattle in to the auctions. Other farmers come there to buy cattle. Farmers who have too many cattle for their grass supply, sell; farmers who have more grass than they have cattle, buy. This system was utilized in Alberta this year. To make cattle available we were prepared to buy them at those sales. We did not have to buy very many. There was only one other province in which it became advisable to encourage the same kind of thing, and that was due largely to the difficulties we had in getting meat out of that province. That was the province in which the disease was found.
We put on some auction sales there, and we did buy a few cattle. Our intention was to put those cattle on pastures, if necessary. I do not think we got any on the pastures. I have heard of one bull that we got on the pasture, but I do not think we got any other cattle on the pasture. We bought some cattle at these sales, but before we got them

Supply-Agriculture
away from the yards some farmer came along and took them to his pasture at a little higher price, or some packer came along and bought them if they were fit for killing. We got rid of them in that way, so we did not actually get any on these pastures, so far as I know. I say that here to give some publicity to it because of the criticism I heard the other day. Some Ontario farmer who was purchasing livestock made the remark, "What kind of market are we going to have this fall when the government has put 10,000 cattle on pasture out west, and will bring them on the market?"
That could have happened, but it did not happen. We agreed to buy the cattle. We did not get them. We have not been getting cattle largely because of the fact that we had the British agreement, and the meat has been moving. Instead of getting cattle, we are getting meat. That meat is going out of the country from day to day and is being disposed of. It is therefore quite proper to say that the offer is made to buy meat at floor prices at the Vancouver plant, the same as it is at other plants. I think now that probably is true at all plants right across the country; the offer is there to buy.
The fact is that we are not getting much right now. We cleared the markets in the few weeks down to the point where we are not getting much right now. This is the time of the year when we hope we do not get much. After all there is a certain amount of stored meat that still has to be sold on this market, in addition to the meat that is being sold over in the old land. We hope to get our storages cleared down to as low a level as possible before the rush of cattle starts to come in toward the end of September, on into October and for the remaining months of the year. We are therefore not overly anxious to have cattle brought into the plants or to the government at present. The farmers also are not overly anxious to bring them in, and they do not do so.
To come to our friends at Kamloops, may I say there is nothing in the world to prevent the farmers at Kamloops from doing the same thing the farmers in Alberta did. Probably there is nothing in the world to prevent this government from doing the same thing there as they did at a number of points in Saskatchewan. If they feel inclined to do so, the farmers themselves can put on an auction. If they do so, I am quite sure the government would not hesitate to put in a buyer at that auction, as I think they have done in the last week, under some pressure, at Lloydminster, where they would buy, I presume, from either side of the provincial
TMr. Gardiner.]
boundary line. But that plant at Lloydmin-ster is privately owned and operated. They have asked to have a government buyer sent there in order to offer to buy live animals at that market, the same as is done at other auctions.
I think that could be arranged at Kamloops. I do not know of any reason why it could not be arranged. It could be arranged either with government support or without it. The fact that we are prepared to buy meat at a floor price down at Vancouver means that they have established for them the floor price at which the animals can be sold in Kamloops, shipped down to Vancouver and slaughtered. We will take the meat there at the floor price. There is nothing to prevent people in any part of British Columbia from organizing themselves and getting that done, just as they have organized in other provinces to have it done in their own way and under the system they are accustomed to.
I do not think I need to say anything more in order to indicate that we are attempting at least to have the same set-up right across the country and to co-operate with those who have animals to sell in order to see to it that the prices are about the same. I think the best indication that we are successful is to be found in the newspaper reports of the markets. I consult the papers every morning when I come to my office. I flndi that the markets are a little bit above the floor right from one end of Canada to the other, and considerably above the floor for the higher qualities of beef. I think that means that the Canadian public is prepared to bid a higher price for the choice beef than they are prepared to bid for some of the lower grades of beef that are being shipped to other markets. It seems to indicate that we in this country prefer the choicer cuts. We are probably paying 28 to 29 cents now for choice steers whereas a short time ago we could not get better than 24 or 25 cents.

From the minister's answer do I understand that instructions have now been issued to the packers operating in British Columbia as to how they should apply the support price to cattle originating in the province and offered to them for sale, whether it be for domestic marketing or for shipment under the four-way meat deal?

What actually happens is this. The only thing we buy is for the fourway meat deal. But the fact that we pay the floor price for that meat makes it impossible for anybody to get anything there at any lower price than the one we pay. We buy all the surplus that is there at that price.

That order has gone to those packing plants just the same as it has gone to every other packing plant in Canada.
With respect to cattle originating in British Columbia?

Yes; with respect to cattle originating in British Columbia or no matter where they originate. As long as the cattle are slaughtered in that plant we are prepared to buy the surplus beef at the floor price. If somebody else comes along and offers more, of course we do not get them, and that meat either stays on the British Columbia market or it could be shipped back further into Canada; but I venture to say that most of it stays on that market.

Just in conclusion may I say the point I was concerned about was my information that with respect to cattle originating in Alberta and Ontario and marketed in British Columbia, the instructions were clear as to how the support price was to be applied; but with respect to cattle originating in British Columbia and marketed in British Columbia the packers had no instructions and were under the impression, according to their advice to the gentleman I have spoken about already, that the lack of instructions must mean they did not have any floor price to apply in British Columbia. If the minister's answer to me is that instructions have now been issued to packers operating in British Columbia in such form that it is clear to them that the support price does apply in British Columbia with respect to cattle originating there and marketed locally as well as to those marketed or bought for the United Kingdom-New Zealand agreement, then I think that will deal with the situation. But I wanted to have it clear from the minister's answer that those instructions have now been issued.
My understanding is that there were never any other instructions issued. But I cannot be responsible for the stories that some buyers of cattle may circulate in British Columbia or anywhere else.

Mr. Chairman, that is not what I said. I said that this gentleman visited at least five packing plants in British Columbia and spoke to their officials, and that was the information given him by all five.

I am not denying that. All I am saying to the hon. member now is that I cannot follow all of those who may be interested in buying cattle at a lower price for any organization that is slaughtering cattle, whether it is a packing plant or whatever it may be. But the fact is that in every 55704-244J
Supply-Agriculture
packing plant in this country there is a standing order to buy beef at the floor price; and there is no line drawn between what is marketed locally and what is marketed through the British contract. We have a standing agreement to buy. If, by some means or other, somebody is talking some people into selling them at a lower rate, I cannot be responsible for that.

The weights and classifications which were issued to the packers, according to this information, covered only cattle originating in Alberta and Ontario. The minister himself has referred to this question of the weights which the department indicated they were prepared to support because they were concerned with those animals which had been prepared for the United States market; and it was those weights which they covered first. As I say, the packers had instructions with regard to those weights but only with respect to animals originating in Alberta and Ontario. Up to the time of my last letter, which was dated June 20, corresponding instructions with regard to animals of comparable weights originating in British Columbia had not been received at the packing plants there.

What I mean by saying it has been true from the beginning is this. It has been true from the beginning of the period when the embargo was removed by British Columbia. We certainly did not go into British Columbia to buy meat at a time when they said they would not take cattle out of Alberta, or they would not take cattle from somewhere else. We said, "We will go in there and buy the meat from cattle brought in and slaughtered." During that period I am sure my hon. friend would not be interested in what happened because their cattle were selling-
The embargo has been removed since the beginning of June or earlier; but the situation I refer to-the absence of instructions-applied, as I say, up to at least June 20.
Let us say that it does nol apply now and it has not applied for some time.
If the minister is making the statement that instructions have now been issued, then he has answered my question. I am sorry it has taken us so long to arrive at that point.
We are all sorry.

In reply to a suggestion made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South

Supply-Agriculture
with respect to the extension of the principle of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, the minister mentioned the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act. I know this comes under another item in the estimates, but I have to be away for a couple of days next week and I thought perhaps I would miss the item when it came up.
Since I come from a district which has received benefit in a material way from this act I think I should congratulate the minister and the officials of his department who are administering the act on behalf of the residents of Albert county in my constituency who are benefiting. At the same time I should like to know whether the minister can give me any assurance that the project which has been suggested, namely that of damming the Shepody river in Albert county, which will result in the reclamation of some thousands of acres of good farm land and give a somewhat better development to many more thousands of acres, will receive the real consideration of the minister and the officials of his department in the early future.

I was wondering whether we could revert from the maritimes back to Vancouver beef. I was surprised to hear criticism of the arrangements that have been made by the interdepartmental committee, particularly with respect to the province of British Columbia. If there is one province or one particular area in which the interdepartmental committee, which is an excellent committee, has done work it is in my own province of British Columbia. There was for a period of some two days no provision for packers in the Vancouver area to kill the heavy meat out of Alberta, but that was corrected by the committee. A man named Mr. Hall of the Department of Trade and Commerce took up immediately with the shipping companies out of the port of Vancouver the question of providing reefer space via the canal, and the matter of rates; and Mr. Evans of the Furness Withy line and the Vancouver secretary of the Pacific conference took up with the shippers the matter of bringing in a rate that would give shipments out of Alberta to Vancouver via the canal a comparable position with reefer car shipments to Montreal and then reefer shipments across the Atlantic.
As a result of the efforts of that committee and the co-operation of the shipping companies we are in a position where Vancouver today has the advantage of 70 cents per hundred. The result is that one packer alone picked up 2,700 heavies, and I believe he raised the price by going into that market and picking them up in that way. We are
[Mr. Riley.j
very well pleased in the province of British Columbia. We [DOT] are customarily buyers of large quantities of Alberta meat, and I think most of the people in British Columbia realize that the most severe situation at that time existed in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. Our response in taking meat out, whether going east or west, relieved the situation in those provinces, and I think this is one of the best jobs the government has ever done. We could have had utter chaos in the meat business if that were not done.
I am going to say this. Notwithstanding the fact that I come from a riding and represent a people where there are no cows or chickens at all, I realize that the thing that keeps this country together is workingmen's wages plus the annual crop on Canadian farms, the cash crop. If these can be kept in proper balance and proper relationship one to the other we will have good times in this country. If either fails we will not have good times. I think the department's work in this matter of marketing and sustaining the prices of meat in Canada until the United States market is open again should be praised by everyone in this House of Commons, not only those from those areas which are producing meat in vast quantities but from all of British Columbia, because the economy of one part depends upon the economy of all. We particularly in British Columbia, I repeat, have been admirably well treated by this interdepartmental committee and the officials down here.

I want to ask the minister a question to clear my own thinking, because I have had a few letters recently in regard to freight assistance. I wrote back what I thought was right. I am now beginning to wonder whether I really was right. I thought that whoever was getting grain by way of purchase at the head of the lakes paid approximately $6 a ton freight on it, and then the government paid the rest of the assistance. I should like the minister to tell me whether I am right or wrong. If I am wrong, will the minister be good enough to put the regulations on Hansard, then I shall look over my correspondence and correct the mistakes I have made.

That is approximately so. It is as near to the exact thing as can be stated. What the hon. member has said to those who have written to him is correct. As I understand it, the freight is paid by the person who ships grain out in western Canada. The freight down to Fort William on the grain is charged against him. Then the government pays the freight from Fort William

to the central point in the east from which it is distributed to farmers in the different areas to which it is shipped. It may not work out at our paying exactly all the freight, but it works out very closely to that.

The point I want to clear up is this. The man or the company getting the grain in Montreal, in Newfoundland or in Prince Edward Island, pays only approximately $6 a ton, and the government pays the rest?
No; we are presumed to be paying the freight from Fort William east to the point from which it is distributed locally. We do not pay the local freight. That is different.
Just at the main point?

But we only pay it provided we are satisfied that the feeder of the grain gets the benefit. If it is demonstrated to us that the person who is handling the grain gets the benefit, that he does not pass it on, we would refuse to pay. The intention of the whole policy is that the freight assistance is given to the feeder of the grain, not to anybody who is handling in between or anyone in that position. The intention is that we pay the freight from Fort William to the distribution point, let us say Montreal or Toronto or dfferent points in Ontario and Quebec, and the same applies to the maritimes.

I wish to commend the minister on the policy he established in setting up auctions in the province of Saskatchewan to purchase cattle. Some time during the discussion I should like the minister to give us the points at which these sales are made or where the auction points were established, and the numbers and grades of cattle purchased at them. The minister may not have the information now, but he can give it sometime later.

So far as I know there are four points up to the present time, Yorkton, Prince Albert, Battleford and Lloydminster. The committee is under instructions to set up the organization whenever it can be properly set up. That requires weighing facilities and everything that is necessary in connection with the handling of stock under those circumstances. But an application would have to be made in the first place. Our arrangement is with the livestock branch of the Saskatchewan pool. They have been authorized to put them in wherever the facilities are available, and where they can put them in.
Supply-Agriculture

Mr. Chairman, I think the discussion yesterday and this afternoon, since the estimates of this department have been before the committee, has been most profitable. Indeed, this has been the most interesting discussion on agriculture generally since I have come to parliament. Hon. members appreciate the fact, Mr. Chairman, that you have given them considerable leeway by way of permitting a free discussion of their problems on this item.
Agriculture is a vital industry in Canada. I would ask permission to speak for two or three moments to place before the minister some thoughts that have occurred to me. Yesterday and today the position of agriculture in Canada has been fully discussed, and we have heard reference to the number of abandoned farms, particularly in the maritime provinces. I might add that this situation also applies, to a certain extent, in that part of Ontario from which I come. To my mind, however, it is not so much a matter of abandoned farms as the condition of those farms across the country. When our United States friends come to visit us in Ontario, they are unfavourably impressed by the unpainted buildings and the fact that the condition of our farms is not what it should be. I believe the same can be said of the condition we find as we travel across the country.
The farmer offers perhaps the greatest single market in this country for industrial production; no one will question that statement. If a farmer has an income of $5,000 or $6,000 a year, he will spend it. If he needs additional equipment, if he must make extensive repairs, he will spend the money on it. Hon. members can depend upon it that if the farmer has money, he will spend it for needed supplies. It was suggested this afternoon by the hon. member for Melfort that cost of feed constitutes an important item in the economy of agriculture. There can be no doubt as to the truth of that statement. It is my view that at its central experimental station the department might give greater and more serious consideration to these feed costs. With the farm prices beginning to come down, as compared with what they were, farmers now find that costs of operation are more burdensome. I trust that this fact will have the serious consideration of the government.
Then this afternoon the minister referred to agricultural prices support. I was pleased to listen to the discussion, and to have the minister's explanation. The Agricultural Prices Support Act was passed in 1944. Hon. members will be surprised to learn the small amount of money spent for this purpose.

Statements on Alleged Germ Warfare Figures show that from 1944 until March of 1951 less than $10 million has been spent for the support of agricultural prices. I agree with the minister's statement that there may be some people in the country who are opposed to the support of agricultural prices. I believe it can be said, however, that speaking generally people throughout the country, including our urban friends, now realize the importance of agriculture to the economy of this country, and are willing to have this important industry get a square deal. I trust the minister will give serious consideration to the matter of price support whenever occasion arises.
Anyone who voices criticism of the amounts spent for the support of agricultural prices in this country will be interested to know what this same process has cost the United States government. From a percentage standpoint, price support for the products of Canadian farms amounted to only one-seventh of one per cent of the national income, up to March 31, 1951. On the other hand 12 per cent has been paid out of the coffers of our American friends for a similar purpose. This is a most significant figure, and will be of particular interest to our urban friends who are now beginning to realize the importance of agriculture in our economy. It will be clear to them at once that, on this comparative basis, the support of agricultural prices has not cost this country anything like the amount of money some people had believed.
Those are the only two comments I wished to make at this time. I have further questions to ask, but I shall be content to ask them when the items are called. I would impress upon hon. members the fact that agriculture is the one industry in Canada that must have support. The Agricultural Prices Support Act is there for that purpose and, in the light of the figures I have indicated, no one can criticize the amount of money that has been spent or may be spent in the future for this purpose.

speechtext:
I should like to make a supplementary statement concerning Dr. James Endicott. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), to whom it was first sent, has forwarded to me a convincing rebuttal of Dr. Endicott's libellous and false charges that the United States has been guilty of bacteriological warfare in Korea and northeast China. It is the work of three distinguished Canadian entomologists, namely, Dr. W. H. Brittain, F.R.S.C., F.A.I., viceprincipal, dean of faculty and professor of entomology, Macdonald college, McGill university; Dr A. W. Baker, B.S.A., head of the department of entomology and zoology of the Ontario agricultural college, and Dr. C. E. Atwood, M.S.A., professor of zoology, university of Toronto.
When, on Wednesday last, in replying to questions previously asked by members of the opposition concerning Dr. Endicott, I justified the government's policy in relation to him in part upon the principles of freedom of speech and freedom of the press, I did not expect that there would be available within four days a clear vindication of these principles.
None of these scientists is in the employ of the federal government. As free men in a free society, without any sort of government compulsion, direction or inspiration, they have, upon their own initiative, produced this reply to Dr. Endicott's untruths concerning bacteriological warfare and, having produced it, turned it over at once to the parliament and the government of their country.
The statement of Drs. Brittain, Baker and Atwood is so important a contribution to this bacteriological warfare question that I propose to lay it upon the table with sufficient copies to supply all of the members of the house and the press gallery.

We shall first study Bill No. 364, to incorporate the Canadian Shipowners Mutual Assurance Association. This bill has been considered by the standing committee on banking and commerce and has been reported without amendment.
On section 1-Incorporation.

It is my understanding that this bill is supposed to fit in with the measure passed by the house within the last day or two providing for war risks insurance. Will the sponsor explain to the committee the manner in which the operation will be carried out so the two bills will work together?

The bill under consideration is a private bill for the purpose of forming together the ship owners in Canada who wish to carry insurance on their ships on the high seas against certain war risks. Under normal conditions the marine insurance companies of course issue policies on ships, but when we encounter a state of war or, for that matter, even when we run into conditions of banditry or agitation such as we had on the Suez canal a few months ago, or riot, insurrection, rebellion or anything else of that kind, there is no coverage for the owners of ships. Consequently over 150 years ago, in the early 1800's groups of ship owners in England gathered together and formed associations or clubs through which, in return for a small premium, they shared
Private Bills
the risks on the various ships under insurance among all ship owners.
During the first and second world wars, there being no possibility of Canadian ship owners having that type of insurance in Canada, our ship owners were obliged to go to the United States or the United Kingdom and insure with one of these clubs or associations. It is a matter of pride that the Canadian marine fraternity are now strong enough and numerous enough and have enough insurable value to form their own club or association, and that they are proposing to do by means of this bill. The bill simply means that in the event of war risks arising or in the event of a state of war coming into existence, ship owners may insure their ships on a mutual basis through this club or association in return for a reasonable premium. The risks are shared by all the ship owners who are members of the association. In turn, inasmuch as a state of war is considered an unnatural state as compared to a peaceful state, it is felt that during wartime it is proper for the government to step in and carry some of the risk for ship owners who may be sailing their ships from one port to another. As I have said, the risks during wartime are unnatural and consequently to cover these risks the government had to set up its own reinsurance scheme, which it did in virtue of Bill No. 336 which was passed here some two or three weeks ago.
In virtue of that bill the government sets aside in the consolidated revenue fund a certain sum against which any charges would be made and from which any payments would come. These unnatural risks which are technically called "queen's enemy risks" are, for example, the following: danger from submarines, from bombing, from mines, from shelling by enemy ships, and from capture by enemy ships. Those particular unnatural risks are covered by the government reinsurance plan. Other extraordinary risks such as attack by pirates, bandits, damage through agitators, riot, insurrection and rebellion would be insured through this association.
I do not know what further details you would like.
Apparently the shipping companies will have to pay a certain premium?
That is right.

I suppose this association would be responsible for a proportion of any loss, or is it a fact that the bulk of the loss would be borne by the government? I do not just understand how the losses are to be shared.

The capital set-up, if I can describe it as such, is fairly simple. Each

Private Bills
ship owner who insures a ship with the association pays a certain premium to the association depending on the value. Let us say for the sake of argument that it is 25 cents per hundred dollars-and my figures are imaginary-of that 25 cents perhaps 5 cents would remain with the association. The difference would go to the government under their reinsurance scheme. It is felt that the annual premiums paid by the various ship owners insured with this club are sufficient to start the association off; then if it is not sufficient, if there were a major loss in the first year for example, members would be prorated for their portion of the loss suffered by one of their members. In other words, it is a straight mutual insurance scheme.
A canvass of ship owners recently made indicated that insurable value to at least $112 million would be available.
Does the government in effect merely act as trustee for the money?

Answering your question obliquely, the government certainly controls the money in its possession and must make a report annually to parliament. If there were very serious losses during a sudden outbreak of war those losses would be paid by the government just the same as other war losses have been paid by the government in the past; so in effect I would imagine the government is trustee of its own moneys and the moneys which will eventually be accumulated by the organization are governed by the board of directors elected by the ship owners themselves.
Are all ship companies in Canada participating in this scheme?

All ship owners have the right to apply and become members, with the exception that the applications of course will be screened by the directors of the association. That is a very wise provision because we might not have people who would be good, honest or desirable risks, just as you have in an ordinary insurance company; so the directors keep to themselves the right to refuse applications. But the record and history of the fraternity of ship owners is such that I do not think there is much danger of that.
Will the association include shipping companies on the great lakes?
Yes, provision is made for shipping companies on the great lakes.
Are they participating actively in this plan? Because it would seem to me that it would make quite a big difference if all shipping on the great lakes as well as deep-sea shipping is to be covered.

My information is that the large ship owners on the Atlantic and on the Pacific are only too willing and in fact anxious to start this scheme, and the lake shipping owners have been approached also and are favourably inclined. There is of course no compulsion used, but they have the opportunity of joining.

I suppose if a ship owner has to become a member of the association, as you say, before he gets advantage of this insurance company, I would take it from reading this bill that this is just another insurance company; only they are looking for business by having as many people as possible join the association. Those who join the association get a lower tariff rate on their insurance. Is that right?

To only a certain degree. The difference between this association and an ordinary marine insurance company is that the ordinary marine insurance company does not insure the risks contemplated by this bill. We are dealing here with war risks, and an ordinary marine insurance company will not insure against war risks. They have a 48-hour cancellation clause and they also decide whether they care to insure at all in the event of war breaking out. At times Canadian ship owners may not be able to get Canadian insurance at all. During the first two wars they were obliged to go to the United States or the United Kingdom to get that extra protection. This association, however, does not compete with ordinary marine insurance.

Another question. How would they operate in comparison with a company like Lloyd's? All our marine insurance, or a great portion of it, goes through that great Lloyd's concern. Would this company that you are promoting here have the same kind of insurance on the cargoes as well as the boats themselves, and can it be taken out at any time without inspection, just the same as you apply for marine insurance at any time with Lloyd's? You can call them up on the telephone and say: My ship is sailing with a cargo valued at so much, and they tell you then and there whether it is covered from the moment you telephone them. Would this company be operated on the regular basis of a concern like Lloyd's or similar agencies?

My information is that it will not compete with Lloyd's. As I have tried to point out, there is a difference between ordinary commercial marine insurance and marine insurance during a state of war or conditions approaching a state of

war. The Minister of Finance in explaining the government measure used certain phraseology which might prove of interest here. It appears on page 3127 of Hansard of June 11. He stated in effect that when Canadian ship owners were obliged to insure with English companies their claims were paid in sterling and under present conditions that is not very satisfactory to Canadian ship owners. Then, too, the English operators place limits on the amount of insurance which Canadian ship owners can obtain. Then again the cost of replacement is much higher in Canada. Frequently Canadian ship owners found themselves without sufficient insurance when they sustained losses. These are advantages that this bill will give to the Canadian ship owner. There will be the settlement of his loss in Canadian funds and the replacement of his ship in Canadian shipyards.

Is it the intention that government-owned ships will come under this plan? I think that is quite an important factor, because at the present time there are a large number of ships owned by the government or by crown companies. I presume in the event of another war most of the deep-sea cargo vessels would be owned by a government agency. Will this government fleet be participating in the scheme or is it to be restricted to vessels owned by private companies?
I cannot answer that directly, but I have reason to believe that government ships will not participate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister answered that question when I put it to him during the debate on the government bill. He said they would not come under this plan.
The minister says, at page 3129 of Hansard for June 11, 1952, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Greenwood:
I notice the minister said that government-owned ships would not participate in any way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not mean government-owned
ships, I meant government-owned aircraft.
I can only deduce from that that government-owned ships would not be participating.
Would not participate?
Would not. I would not want to guarantee that, but I have seen nothing to indicate that they would be included.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Powers of the association.

Paragraph (a) of section 3 contains the broad general powers of this association, and they do not seem to be restricted
Private Bills
to war risks. Is the intention that there can only be insurance against war risk or is power taken by the association to give a broader coverage?

Well, certainly the
first intention is against war risks. As a general thing in granting charters the legal lights try to include as many powers as they can because you cannot always anticipate every move in the future. After reading these powers, I believe they are in the general terms we usually get in a charter granted by the Secretary of State. Frankly, 1 do not see any contradiction in these general powers. Naturally, when you insure a ship you also have cargo inside the ship and you have other things pertaining to the ship; that is why they are set out in detail.

The point I am making is that the powers seem to be broad enough to enable the association to do insurance business. It is not restricted to war risks. There is no mention in that section that I can see of war risks. It just refers to general risks of various kinds. I do not see any mention of war risks at all.

In reply I can only say that the marine insurance business has been established for many years. The people following the business are rather skilful, and there has been no pressure by the established marine insurance companies to change the wording of this paragraph. I think they are quite satisfied that this association is not going to enter into active competition, certainly at the present or in the foreseeable future.

Section agreed to.
Section 4 agreed to.
On section 5-Board of directors.
This section provides for the board of directors. Is there any plan in contemplation for dividing the directors between the east coast shipping, St. Lawrence shipping and the west coast?

The first directors of the association are set forth in section 1. One of them comes from Westmount, one from Hampstead, one from Montreal, one from Montreal West, one from Vancouver and one from Halifax. Those are the provisional incorporators and first directors. You will have noticed that there can be up to 21 directors, so the leeway affords opportunity of adding directors across the country.

What is the capital of this company? What security have the insured? I do not see any mention here of the amount of capital they have; or do they reinsure all their risks?

Private Bills

There is no actual mention of capital because this is a mutual association. The members who are accepted, the ship owners, pay a certain premium on the value of their ships, and that is how the association gets its money to finance operations. In the event of a disaster, all the members are prorated in proportion to the value of their ships, so you have the net worth of each ship owner as a guarantee against the risks of the whole association. The reinsurance provision, subject to correction, I think is up to 95 per cent with the government.

Section agreed to.
Sections 6 to 15 inclusive agreed to.
On section 16-Director may contract with the association.
Can the sponsor explain that provision in section 16 which seems to enable a director to make a personal contract direct with the association?

I would hesitate to give any direction to learned counsel facing me, because I am sure he can interpret that better than I can. If the hon. member cares to read subparagraphs 3 and 4 I think he will find sufficient precautions are inserted. Actually, I do not know what the technical reason is, but once a contract is made the director concerned must declare his interest in it in virtue of this section, and then I think he has complied with it sufficiently both morally and legally.

Section agreed to.
Sections 17 to 21 inclusive agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

that the house go into committee to consider Bill No. 365, an act to incorporate Ogdensburg bridge authority.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

Apparently the plan of the applicants for this charter is to build a bridge over the St. Lawrence river. I should like to know from the sponsor just how that is going to fit in with the St. Lawrence seaway and power development, whether the bridge will be in that area of the river, and whether

the plan is to proceed with the construction before the waterway and power projects are developed.

Section 11 explains that any plans must be submitted to the government and passed upon before they are accepted. They must conform with all requirements of navigation. Although the proposed location has not been decided upon, according to this bill the bridge must be built within five miles either east or west of the city of Ogdensburg in the state of New York or the town of Prescott in the province of Ontario. That means the bridge itself will be well above any of the proposed seaway construction.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 and 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Capital stock.

This company is to have capital stock of $1 million divided into 100,000 common shares without nominal or par value. It is not stated whether this $1 million or any portion of it is to be paid up or ever will be paid up. This stock may only be there for sale to those who may be looking for some stock to buy. I should like the sponsor of the bill to explain that provision a little more thoroughly.

As to this clause 4, referring to the $1 million of capital stock divided into 100,000 common shares, we find that this method is similar to the method in the bill with respect to the Thousand Islands Bridge Company, which was passed in this house in 1934 and amended in 1935. In that case-and we have every reason to believe the situation will be the same in this one-when the companies were amalgamated the stock was absorbed by the United States company. The bonds were sold in the United States. The financing was all done in the United States. No Canadian money was involved in any way. The stock can either be paid for outright by the directors or it can be sold on the market, or it can be acquired through the purchase of debentures, but ultimately it will be retired, along with any bonds or debentures, and the bridge will then be turned over to Canada and New York state free of encumbrance.

The purpose of this money
is for the building of this bridge, is it not?
Yes.
What is the cost of the bridge estimated at? What is it going to cost?

There is a limit set in this bill, by clause 12, subsection 1. That limit

is an amount which must not exceed $12 million. I might say that was an amendment made in the Senate. Originally it was $10 million and the Senate increased it by $2 million in case, when the bridge was finally built, it was found that it was going to cost more than the engineers' estimate.

Section agreed to.
Sections 5 to 9 inclusive agreed to.
On section 10-Tolls and revenues.
No provision is made in this section as to the amount of the tolls. Should there be some regulation there for the purpose of limiting what the tolls could be in a case of this kind?

Inasmuch as there are ferries running, and inasmuch as there are two other bridges not too far away from this one, it would not be to the advantage of the company to charge tolls in excess of the tolls charged by the ferries. When I say the "ferries" I mean the ferries that operate elsewhere than from Ogdensburg to Prescott. I believe they will not charge tolls in excess of the tolls charged by the Roosevelt bridge at Cornwall or the Thousand Islands bridge at Ivy Lea. It is not reasonable to suppose that any corporation is going to charge prices that will drive the travelling public to some other way of getting across the St. Lawrence river.

Judging from the answer given by the sponsor of the bill I would take it that the setting of the tolls is entirely in the discretion of the directors of the bridge company. Is there not the necessity of going to the board of transport commissioners and obtaining a ruling on the reasonableness of these tolls?

The tolls come under the jurisdiction of the Railway Act. Naturally the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada will ultimately be required to set the maximum tolls payable, as will also the corresponding body in the United States.
It is perfectly clear that the board of transport commissioners will have the power to regulate these tolls?
Oh, definitely.

Section agreed to.
On section 11-Location of bridge.

I should like to know just what the length of this bridge will be. What is the estimated length of it when completed? If this bridge is a great success, and if it can be built for $10 million or $12 million, I cannot help thinking that in
Private Bills
our part of our country we might be interested in a similar proposition with respect to a bridge to connect us up with the mainland. What would be the length of this bridge?

The width of the St. Lawrence river in that district-that is in the area five miles east of Prescott and five miles west of Prescott-is almost an even mile. Not being an engineer, and not having seen the engineer's plan, I do not know how long the approaches will be. But as to the United States approach of the Thousand Islands bridge, where they have to go up from the river level to the height required for navigation purposes, it is just under half a mile.
A third of the distance.

Section agreed to.
Sections 12 and 13 agreed to.
On section 14-Amalgamation with other companies.
Section 14 gives power to amalgamate with other companies. Is it the intention of the sponsors of this bill to amalgamate with a United States company?

With respect to an international bridge such as this, the usual practice is to have a Canadian company formed for the purpose of attending to the construction costs. But when the bridge is open for traffic, either the Canadian company can absorb the United States company for administration purposes or the United States company can absorb the Canadian company. The financial obligations of the one company immediately become the obligations of the other company.
What United States company are the sponsors going to amalgamate with in this case?

The company that has been set up and authorized by the New York state legislature. When the act was passed in May of this year it set up an authority with the power to raise the necessary funds in the United States. It is a private authority. The bonds do not have any government backing in any way. I understand, however, that a traffic survey was made by the state of New York before the New York state assembly passed this act allowing the authority to be created, and it was found that the traffic to be served would warrant the expenditure of a large sum of money to complete a bridge between Ogdensburg and Prescott. Therefore, with this blessing, there is no reason why the authority as set up in the state of New York cannot raise its funds

Private Bills
through the usual financial channels-banks, trust companies or otherwise

in the United States. I do not anticipate that any money will be raised in Canada.
What is the name of that authority?

The Ogdensburg bridge
authority.

Section agreed to.
Sections 15 to 17 inclusive agreed to.
On section 18-Time for commencement and completion of bridge.

I understand there are two other bridges across this same river. Is there any guarantee that there will not be any interference with smaller boats going up and down the river, or is there allowance for that? One would think that in this day and age, instead of building a bridge they would consider plans for a tunnel. Have any figures been prepared on the cost of a tunnel as compared with a bridge?

There should be no difficulty in respect to obstructing navigation for smaller ships. As I explained earlier, at this point the river is approximately a mile wide. There are wide channels that have a good depth. I would say the river is between 50 feet and 70 feet in depth. The very fact that the river is so deep at this point precludes the possibility of a tunnel ever being built at a reasonable figure. I believe the cost of the tunnel would be away out of line.

Do the plans ensure that this will be a safe bridge? The Duplessis bridge in another part of the country collapsed with great loss of property and life. I hope the plans provide for a bridge that will stand up.

Inasmuch as bridges come under the authority of the board of transport commissioners and the corresponding body in the United States, the hon. member can rest assured that the plans when finally approved will guarantee the bridge to be perfectly safe.

Section agreed to.
Sections 19 to 24 inclusive agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
Title agreed to.	.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
