speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DIVORCE BILLS-CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE- THIRD READINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the motion for clause 1 of these bills carries may I just say a word with respect to these bills, as part of the rather large batch of divorce bills we have put through at this session. This may be the last night of this session that we shall be dealing with divorce bills, and I should imagine hon. members would be interested in a few statistics as to what we have done with respect to divorce cases in the House of Commons during the current session.
If and when we pass these 70 bills, clause 1 of which is now before us, we shall have passed in this House of Commons 312 divorce bills. The Senate passed 313. I understand that the miscellaneous private bills committee turned down one of the bills which the house referred to it. That figure of 312 bills is the second largest number of divorces to be dealt with in any session of parliament. Hon. members will probably be interested as well in the amount of time that we have spent in this session on divorce bills. I have checked the record, and I find that tonight is the seventeenth occasion during this session of parliament that we have dealt with divorce bills. They were reached three times on Mondays and fourteen times, including tonight, on Tuesdays and Fridays.

Private Bills-Divorce
I have also acertained that the total amount of time we have spent on divorce bills on these seventeen occasions, including ten minutes that might be taken this evening, adds up to five hours and twenty-five minutes. Now, it takes only a little bit of simple arithmetic to ascertain that if we have spent five hours and twenty-five minutes on 313 divorce bills it means that we have dealt with divorce bills at all the stages that concern us in the House of Commons, first reading, second reading, committee stage and third reading, in an average of one minute and two seconds per divorce. But, Mr. Chairman, as the hon. members know-

maintopic: DIVORCE BILLS-CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE- THIRD READINGS
speechtext: How long did the Senate take?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DIVORCE BILLS-CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE- THIRD READINGS
speechtext:
-averages are deceiving. The hon. member asks how long the Senate takes. Perhaps he can go to the Senate and find out, but I am concerned about the way in which we observe our responsibilities as members of the House of Commons. I was saying that averages are deceiving. Perhaps it is not fair to say that we have dealt with divorces in an average of one minute and two seconds per divorce, because actually out of that five hours and twenty-five minutes which we spent altogether in the House of Commons on divorce we spent four hours and thirty-five minutes on 22 cases. In other words, these 22 cases actually had the attention of the House of Commons for an average of twelve minutes each. But that means the other 291 divorces were dealt with in this House of Commons in a total of fifty minutes, which means that the average time spent on each was ten seconds. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that that is not a very commendable record for the House of Commons-ten seconds per divorce-regardless of what may be said of the Senate.
To be completely fair there is a further bit of time that perhaps should be added to this, namely the time spent by the miscellaneous private bills committee. I am not a member of that committee and I have no record of the time spent on them; but a little calculation suggests that even if you add that time in it would extend by only a few seconds the average time spent by the House of Commons in all of its stages on these divorces.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that one thing has to happen. Either some other way should be found for dealing with these divorce cases than by parliament, or we should take our responsibilities more seriously. I note that this matter has been commented on in the editorial columns of both Ottawa newspapers today. One of them even suggests that the Senate might go on strike and leave the job to us. As a matter of fact that is a


suggestion of which the senators might well take note. Perhaps if we really had to do the job in this house hon. members might face up more seriously to the nature of the task and to the desirability of finding some other tribunal for it.
There is one other statistic I should like to give to the committee, Mr. Chairman. I have here the booklets of evidence and the bills for the 313 cases we have handled this session. It is a shameful pile, someone says; a perfectly apt remark. There it is, on the top of my desk, and it measures fifteen inches high. But this is just the pile furnished to me. The same pile is supplied to all of us. There are 262 members of the House of Commons and 102 of the Senate-364 members of parliament altogether. If one multiplies the bills I have here by 364 it would produce a stack of divorce evidence and divorce bills-and that is in English only, because the evidence is not printed in French, although the bills are-that would be 455 feet high.
That figure may not mean very much to the ordinary person. With that in mind I inquired of our good friends at the main door who know the statistics about this building and ascertained before I came to the chamber at eight o'clock the height of the peace tower. They tell me the peace tower is 300 feet high, right up to the very base of the flagpole. So I suggest to hon. members that when they are walking up to the building tomorrow morning they should just take a look at that peace tower, 300 feet high, and realize that this session's divorce evidence and divorce bills make a pile half again as high as the peace tower, or 455 feet high.

maintopic: DIVORCE BILLS-CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE- THIRD READINGS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Royal says they would reach right up to heaven. Perhaps he is thinking in the wrong direction. I do suggest it might be an additional tourist attraction in this city if, when our tourists come to admire the parliament buildings and admire the height of the peace tower, there could be on one side of the tower piled up for them that 455 feet of divorce bills and evidence with which we have dealt in the House of Commons, at the average rate of one minute and two seconds per divorce, so the people of this country may see that evidence of this phase of our work.
I know none of us likes handling this business. None of us really feels that this is the place to deal with the cases we have before us tonight. I hope that as hon. members contemplate that record of one minute and two seconds per divorce-really only ten seconds per divorce for 291 of them-and as hon. members contemplate that picture of a

stack of bills and evidence 455 feet high, they will decide next session to join with me and with members of the Senate who have once again this week made the same recommendation, in finding a way to get divorce bills out of parliament and before some other tribunal.

speechtext: Shall item No. 1 carry?

3. Advisory committee on agricultural services, $5,000.
Are films produced under this item for the Department of Agriculture?
Films are produced by the film board for the Department of Agriculture.
How many were produced last year?
Two were finished that were started the year before, and one new one.
Who are the personnel of this advisory committee?
The deputy ministers of the different provinces, the chief officials of the agricultural colleges, and the chief officials of our own department.

What work have they taken on in an advisory capacity? I have heard of them acting only once, and that was in connection with a position that could not be handled by the civil service commission, when an appointment was made.
They meet and discuss the whole range of activities, both provincially and federally, of the provincial and federal departments. They advise upon methods of dealing with problems.
They are not paid a salary or anything?

Just travelling expenses.

Science service administration-
6.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $1,331,525.
The new science building at the experimental station at Charlottetown would come under this item so far as its completion is concerned. I understand it is not quite complete.
We expect to have it finished in October.
The new science building?
Yes.
Would it be under this item that the money would be spent on the buildings at Grosse lie, or what item would that come under?
Expenditures on Grosse lie are made by the defence board. There are arrangements entered into between this country and the United States.
What new buildings and new equipment are being provided at the experimental farm at Nappan?

Item agreed to.
Animal pathology-
7.	Operation and maintenance, $462,546.

In view of some of the statements we have seen in the press in the last month, I wonder if the minister would say if there is any truth with respect to the statements about the animal diseases research institute in Hull. Is any consideration being given by the government to moving that laboratory from Hull?

There has never been any suggestion so far as I know upon which to base any statements that the laboratory is going to be moved. The only discussions that have taken place with respect to it had to do with what might happen in connection with the checks that are made on foot-and-mouth disease. Nothing else was discussed with respect to it.
It was just the fact that the diagnosis might be carried on at Grosse lie instead of at Hull.

There is no question so far as diagnosis is concerned under the policy that has been followed up to now and which, so far as I know, is still going to be followed. The policy is to have the diagnosis made on

Supply-Agriculture
the premises where the disease develops, but other tests that may be made after the diagnosis will in all probability be carried on at Grosse lie, as is being done at present.
I hope they have better luck with their tests in the field than they had last time.
We had very good luck.
Is this the proper item under which to discuss foot-and-mouth disease?
Not again.
Is item No. 7 the proper one under which to discuss foot-and-mouth disease?
No, the proper place to discuss it is under compensation for animals slaughtered. .

Item agreed to.
Animal pathology-
8.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $81,895.
I should like to ask the minister to tell us where the money is being spent. I looked at page 82 but I did not see any details there to tell us where the money is being spent.

The first place is Hull, construction of incinerator, post mortem building, farm section, $4,800. Then there is construction of a root house and paddock building, poultry building and farm section, $4,500. Then there is a storage shed at the main laboratory, $2,000, a passageway connecting the main laboratory and the poultry disease laboratory, $2,000. At Lethbridge there is an addition to the laboratory, $10,000; a six-room bungalow to replace dwelling No. 3, $12,000; a frame house, $4,800. Then there is Vancouver animal quarters, $19,000; acquisition of equipment, $22,795. At Sackville, New Brunswick, there is an expenditure of $675; at Macdonald college, $1,200, and at Ottawa, $100. At Lethbridge, Alberta, there is an expenditure of $8,105; at Vancouver, $2,990 and at Hull, Quebec, another expenditure of $9,725. That is the total amount.

Item agreed to.
9.	Bacteriology and dairy research, $191,189.
Does any testing work so far as checking margarine for moisture and that sort of thing come under this branch?
No.
It does not?
Not for this department.

Item agreed to.

Botany and plant pathology-
10.	Operation and maintenance, $1,233,231.

What headway has been made in cultivating new varieties of potatoes, more particularly at the experimental farm at Fredericton? I understand they have made a specialty of that, and that some headway has been made in securing new varieties which are free from disease. A great many diseases affect potatoes, and it is a very important accomplishment if varieties can be obtained that are free from blight and the different diseases that make such inroads on the raising of potatoes by the growers of the maritime provinces. What progress has been made, and what new varieties have been recommended to the producers of potatoes?
I understand we have developed two new varieties which are blight resistant, but I think we can get the details of that better under experimental farms. It really does not come under this item.	,

Item agreed to.
Entomology-
14. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $124,830.

The report of the Department of Agriculture says that severe outbreaks of spruce budworm resulting in the loss of millions of cords of spruce and balsam in northern Ontario during the past decade have now largely subsided. Will the minister state whether that is completely eradicated at the present time?
No, it has not been eradicated. It is still doing considerable damage in both New Brunswick and Ontario. We are still working on it, of course.

Has the situation
improved at all?
Yes, it has improved some, but it has not been eradicated.
I would like to ask the minister a similar question with regard to the disease "dieback of birch" from which almost 80 per cent of the birch has died.
There is a team working on it in both Ontario and Quebec, but no final results have been arrived at yet.

I believe forests come under provincial control. Just what is the method worked out between the provinces and the dominion with regard to this department? Do the provinces have to make application to your department for investigations, or just what method is used in co-operating?

We supply the technical and scientific work in investigations such as are carried on in these buildings that are mentioned here, and the provinces look after transportation and actual operations in the field.
In spraying the forests for budworm and other diseases, who looks after the cost of the actual spraying material? Do you pay or do the provinces?
The companies and the provinces co-operate in doing such work as the actual spraying and that kind of thing.

Item agreed to.
Experimental farms service-
18. Experimental farms service administration, $171,213.

Last year I was making inquiries with regard to the experimental farm here. While I have nothing to say about it except that it is a wonderful place for visitors, I often wonder when there is going to be a limit to the increased expenditures. For instance, for a number of years expenditures have been going up at the rate of a quarter of a million dollars a year. I think this year the estimates are a quarter of a million dollars higher but we don't see very much about the revenue derived from it. I would like to find out if the revenue is going up in comparison with the cost as we have it here. Could I have that information?

Well, of course, the expenditure has always been considerably higher than the revenue from government experimental farms in general. That is particularly true of the experimental farm in Ottawa. It is not the intention or at least it is not expected that we will make a profit out of operating an experimental farm. It is an expenditure made by the government of the country for the purpose of giving scientific information after research to farmers in general across the country. It is not intended that we should make a profit out of that. As a matter of fact there is a very considerable cost.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I am quite aware of that and of what a wonderful benefit it is. What I was getting at is that there must be a limit to the increase in cost per year. The total for the head farm here is now $2 million, and with increases of a quarter of a million dollars each year it won't be long until it is a tremendous proposition. We have an experimental station down in our own province, a very wonderful
Supply-A griculture
institution for the benefit of the farmers, and I would like to see a little more money spent down there on that.
Hear, hear.

Another thing, the illustration stations seem to be of more benefit throughout the country than the experimental farms because there are really more people who take advantage of those stations. I would like to know from the minister whether there is going to be an increase in the number of illustration stations in our province.

They are increasing slowly all the time. There are 228 of these illustration stations in the country now. There has not been a tendency to decrease them at any time, and they are increasing in number slowly. I may say that we also consider them to be very valuable. It is not our intention to increase the number of experimental farms, as we have a sufficient number to do the work we think is required in that direction.

I would like to ask the minister if there are any plans for extending the work in the Peace river bloc in British Columbia. I should also like to know what progress has been made at the new experimental farm at Whitehorse. I am told that very valuable work is being done up there and that many things are being found out about the possibilities of food production even at that point in Canada which must be four or five thousand miles from Prince Edward Island.

There are a number of rather important illustration stations up through that country. There is one at Atha-baska Landing which I am quite sure the hon. member would know about, and there are others in the area. There is one very close to Fort St. John, just south of there. The one at Beaverlodge is the largest one close by. It is not in British Columbia; it is on the Alberta side of the boundary. Nevertheless it does serve that part of the country in a big way. Of course it is our desire as settlement moves north in that country to have illustration stations to assist those who are settling there.
Would the minister care to comment on the experimental work in the Yukon Territory?

There is an experimental farm just west of Whitehorse which is carrying on all the usual work carried on at an experimental farm. They have not as much livestock as you can see at some experimental farms, but they have poultry and they are also carrying on experimental work in connection with the growing of

Supply-Agriculture
cereals and grasses of different kinds that are suited to that country. There is good acreage in that farm, but it is only partially cleared.
There are other experimental plots at different places. About thirteen miles out of Dawson City there is one run by a private individual to which we give some assistance. They have some plots for growing cereals, potatoes, vegetables, raspberries and small fruits of different kinds.

I wonder if the minister could tell us the cost of the success that has been derived from the use of the new silo for the dairy barn at the central experimental farm here. It is supposed to be of glass lined construction, and I wonder how it is panning out for various silages.

The experiment which has been carried on with the one at the farm would indicate the cost is comparatively high. It would be probably too high for an individual to utilize to advantage. This is being tried out as an experiment, but at the present time the costs are high.
Could the minister tell us what the cost was?
Around $7,000.
What is the size of it, around 14 by 45?
It is about 14 feet across and 35 feet high.
What is the type of dairy cattle they have at the experimental farm here? Do they specialize in one particular breed, or have they herds of the various breeds of dairy cattle?
At Charlottetown?
No, at the central experimental farm here.
There are two breeds here, Holsteins and Ayrshires.
I suppose Holsteins would compose the larger part of the herd?
About the same of each.

Item agreed to.
Central experimental farm-
20. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $325,765.

The minister spoke about illustration stations this afternoon. I quite agree with his remarks, because I think they are a great benefit to the agricultural community. Can the minister tell me how many new illustration stations were built or put into operation last year?
There were 19 new ones.
Can the minister say how many of those were in the province of Ontario?
The Fort William district, Fort Frances; the eastern and central Ontario district, Chapleau; there are just the two.

Item agreed to.
Branch experimental farms-
21. Operation and maintenance, $5,384,946.

This is the item on which the minister suggested I ask him the question concerning the development of new varieties of potatoes. He stated two varieties had been developed at the experimental farm at Fredericton which the department is now able to recommend to the growers of potatoes. I should like to know if those varieties are now available to potato growers, and I should like to know the names of those varieties. There are the well established varieties such as Irish Cobbler, Green Mountain and a number of others.

There are the two varieties, Canso and Keswick, both of which are blight resistant. They were distributed last year to the growers of seed potatoes, and are now ready for distribution to the public in general through these growers but not from the department. They can be purchased from the growers.
Has any ceiling price been established on these seed potatoes?
No. There are hundreds of growers, however, and there will be some competition in the matter of selling them.
Is the experimental farm able to give growers samples so they might do some planting, or is that done entirely by private growers?
They get them entirely from the private growers.

How do the
private growers get them?
They got them last year from the experimental farm.
Other growers would not be able to get any this year from the experimental farm?
No, the practice has been to do it the way I have suggested, namely to distribute the seed to seed growers during one season; then they multiply the seed and sell it the following year.

Can the minister state the results so far as production per acre

is concerned, that is whether these are good producers or whether they are merely blight resistant?

The records for both quality and production are particularly good. I have not the figures as to quantity, because the potatoes are in the hands of growers all over the area. Our information is that there is a considerable quantity.
Can the minister state where they may be acquired by growers in Nova Scotia?
We can furnish a list of the growers who grew them to anyone who desires to have it. They can buy from whichever one they wish.

Who selects the growers who will propagate the new varieties of grains? Is it the department or the Canadian Seed Growers' Association, or how do you decide to whom you are going to distribute new varieties for propagation purposes.

The same practice is followed with grain that I have just mentioned in connection with potatoes. We produce the varieties, and when we have a certain quantity we put it out to the members of the Canadian Seed Growers' Association and they multiply it. Then they have it for sale.
Who makes the selection of the members of the Canadian Seed Growers' Association to whom these varieties are sent?

They make application directly to the seed growers' association, and we get a recommendation, of course, from that association. Then each person is supplied about equal quantities of the seed and those persons multiply the seed.

What I am trying to get at is who makes the selection. A good bit of money has been made in the propagation and sale of new varieties when they have come on the market in the first place. I should like to know just who makes the selection of the growers to be used in propagating these new varieties. Is it the Canadian Seed Growers' Association executive or your department?

The individual makes his application to the seed growers' association for membership in the association. He makes application for seed probably at the same time. The seed is distributed to him as a member of the association, but he must meet the requirements of the association as a grower before he will be admitted to membership in that organization.

I understand that thoroughly, but there is not enough of these new varieties to send samples to every member of the
Supply-Agriculture
Canadian Seed Growers' Association who may make application. What I want to know is who makes the selection from the growers who make application for the right to propagate these new varieties.

There are two ways of doing the multiplying. We do some of it by contract. Of course where we do it by contract we make the selection ourselves. So far as others are concerned, I understand that it is a case of first come, first served, with no selection made. So long as they are admitted as seed growers by the association, they are entitled to get seed on application, so long as a supply is available. Of course, when we run out, we cannot supply them any further.
Will the minister give us some information with regard to what educational films on agricultural subjects are being sponsored by his department for production by the film board during the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We passed that item.
I gave information with regard to the number a little while ago. Only two were finished, and they were started last year. There is one new one this year. Does the hon. member desire their names?
No.

With regard to the question raised by the hon. member for Melfort, is it not a fact that there are two classes of growers in the seed growers' association? Is there not a list of elite growers who have the preference with regard to obtaining seed?
That is correct; there are the two classes of growers.
I do not think the ordinary member of the Canadian Seed Growers' Association ever gets an opportunity, without passing as an elite grower, to get seed of that first generation seed.
That is the term that is used in describing that particular class of growers. They have the qualifications necessary for the multiplying of seed.
They have the necessary qualifications, certainly. Can the minister tell us how many growers across Canada qualified as elite seed growers?

I am told that it would be difficult to get the figures with regard to that classification, which applies to the different kinds of crops that are grown across the country. They are classified and selected according to their qualifications for growing that particular kind of seed.

Supply-Agriculture

Before six o'clock I asked the minister a question in connection with the establishment of an illustration station at Derwent, Alberta, which is about 25. miles north of Vermilion. When the item was going through I was just returning from a meeting of the redistribution committee, and I was not here to ask it. I wonder if I could get an answer from the minister at this time.
Is it the station at Fort Kent?
At Derwent. It is on the north C.P.R. line between Lloydminster and Edmonton.
One is not established there yet. At least we have not one on record as being established there yet.

About two years ago quite a large number of farmers asked to have one established at that point. They were quite interested, and their interest has not waned as the years have gone by. Will the minister give consideration to the establishment of an illustration station at that point?
We will have that matter investigated.
If the minister will do that I shall be obliged to him.

Item agreed to.
Production service-Health of animals-
24. Administration of Animal Contagious Diseases Act, and Meat and Canned Foods Act, $4,889,025.
Can the minister tell us what success his department is having with the new vaccine for Newcastle disease?

With ithe development of an improved vaccine by the animal diseases research institute it was considered desirable by the Department of Agriculture, after consultation with provincial authorities and the poultry industry, to provide for control of Newcastle disease in poultry by vaccination rather than by the slaughter of infected flocks. Arrangements were made with the provinces of Ontario and Nova Scotia whereby the Department of Agriculture, through the animal diseases research institute, would supply the necessary vaccine and the province would arrange for distribution and application of the vaccine.
The vaccine was used upon an estimated 22 flocks in Nova Scotia and 371 in Ontario, and results to date have indicated that the vaccination program has definite possibilities of success. Newcastle disease broke out in 12 flocks in Nova Scotia and in 35 flocks in Ontario after the vaccine had been administered. In Nova Scotia all flocks in which
the disease occurred were slaughtered; in Ontario this was not considered necessary, as the disease was less virulent. In spite of careful investigation it has not been possible to determine the precise cause of the outbreaks; however, it must be assumed from the incidence of the disease in relation to the vaccination program that it was due to the vaccination or the vaccine.
It is hoped that a continuation of this vaccination program, complemented by the use of live vaccine in young chicks, will lead to a complete termination of ithe relatively costly slaughter and compensation policy. Regular compensation under the animal contagious diseases regulations would not adequately compensate the owners of the hatchery flocks referred to herein, who lost superior quality birds at the beginning of the season of hatching egg production.
Because of the special quality and purpose of the flocks concerned, ithe role of the government in the vaccination program and the importance of retaining the good will of poul-trymen towards vaccination, it is considered desirable to provide special compensation for flock owners who suffered substantial losses by reason of death of birds and lowered production during the hatching season. Competent officers of the Department of Agriculture have appraised the loss sustained by each flock owner; ithe names of the flock owners and the amount of the loss in each case are listed in a schedule attached.

I could not hear everything the minister was saying, but I understood him to say that special compensation was being paid to the owners of flocks that had been slaughtered owing to the vaccination. Did I understand him correctly?
Yes.

Special compensation is
being paid?
The amount is provided in the supplementary estimates which we shall be coming to later.
Compensation is being paid? For whatever loss was occasioned by whatever went wrong with the vaccine, compensation is being paid?
Yes. That is all being paid for.

Do I understand from the minister that no more of the virulent vaccine has been distributed since these unfortunate outbreaks in Nova Scotia? The department has ceased sending out any vaccine of the same type as that which proved to be so faulty in Nova Scotia?
Vaccine is still going out to people who apply for it and desire to use it, and it is having very helpful results.

Evidently not; it could not have helpful results if it infected flocks with Newcastle disease. I gather from what the minister says there has been no similar experience since that which happened in Nova Scotia. I can take from what the minister has said that no Newcastle disease is being induced in flocks through the use of this vaccine.

It has not been established definitely that it was the vaccine that caused the difficulty. There were 12 flocks in Nova Scotia that did develop the disease after the vaccine had been applied, and there were 35 out of 371 in Ontario. The others claimed to have had benefits from it. The question as to what caused the difficulty in that limited number of cases has not been answered.
The disease did not develop in any flocks in which this vaccine was not used.

The disease was in existence before the vaccine was used at all, I understand. That is the reason they went in and started to use it; but not in nearly all the cases where the vaccine was used did the disease develop. As a matter of fact there were far more where it did not develop than where it did, and where it was presumed it did prevent the development of the disease.

I question the information the minister has given. The information I have is that Newcastle disease did not develop in any flocks except those in which this vaccine had been used. I think all the poultry owners and the owners of hatcheries took for granted that Newcastle disease developed because of faulty vaccine, and that vaccine had been used in those flocks as a preventive. It was not used after the Newcastle disease had developed. The owners of the hatcheries were encouraged, induced or persuaded to have the vaccine used as a preventive, not to cure the flocks already infected.

Well, the story is that in the first instance the officials of the department were of the opinion that we should slaughter the poultry, and there was the very strongest of pressure brought to bear upon the department suggesting that it was a waste, and that the poultry should not be slaughtered in order to wipe out the disease. Those who held that opinion of course advocated the use of vaccines. We did get a vaccine from Britain that we had some trouble with in British Columbia, and we had some trouble
Supply-Agriculture
in Nova Scotia with the vaccine that was developed. I think it is correct to say that the disease which did develop in most of the cases followed the application of the vaccine, but there were places or flocks in which the disease developed where no vaccine was used. But of the 22 flocks in which the vaccine was used, 12 developed the disease in Nova Scotia. Much better results were obtained in the province of Ontario than in Nova Scotia. In starting any of these experiments in connection with anything of this kind you always run some risk. It is a matter of experimentation, and when there are losses of course they have to be paid for.

As I understand it, Mr. Chairman, Newcastle disease did not develop in any instance in flocks in Nova Scotia, except where flocks had been vaccinated or had been in direct contact with flocks that had been vaccinated. I think that is the accepted statement in Nova Scotia.

Well, it is not accepted in the department here. Our officials have made a check, and they say there are a number of flocks in Nova Scotia where no vaccine was used but the disease developed. I have not been down there myself and I cannot give you any further information than what I get from the officials.

Will the minister put on record the schedule of payments in compensation for those birds at various ages, and will he tell us how it compares with compensation paid in any states of the United States, if there are any states that pay compensation for this disease at all?

Well, it is quite a big table. I would not like to read it all to the committee. It has been given as a return this session, has it not? If not I can see that it is put on the record as a return. It is correct to say that in the United States they do not pay compensation and they do not slaughter. It is not controlled down there by federal authority.

Would the minister care to comment on the rumour that Newcastle disease has spread to sea birds in the maritimes? Is there any possible grain of truth in that? Will the minister give us an indication of how the compensation paid for poultry destroyed owing to Newcastle disease was arrived at, and how it compares with compensation paid for poultry destroyed on account of foot-and-mouth disease?

To answer the last question first, I understand the same schedule is used in connection with foot-and-mouth disease as the other. There is no evidence to indicate

Supply-Agriculture
whether there is anything to the story that sea gulls have taken the disease. We know nothing of it. On the other point having to do with the basis, the regulations require that the poultry destroyed shall be burned and destroyed absolutely, or deeply buried, one or the other.
Is it not a fact that in the United States they have been vaccinating for this disease for a number of years?

In the United States, as I said a moment ago, it is not done federally. Whatever is done is done in the individual states, and there may be some difference in the manner in which it is done. Anyone can buy the vaccine in the states and use it. Of course if one buys it, he uses it at his own risk.

That would be the reason there is no compensation over there? It has been the accepted practice for some years to vaccinate for Newcastle disease in the United States, and there is no reason why any compensation should be paid. While I am on my feet I should like to ask the minister whether he can give us the standing now of the t.b. testing work being done county-wide across Ontario.

As is well known by hon. members, we took most of the veterinarians who were available across the country out to western Canada, and that has slowed down the program considerably. But in order to indicate what has been going on it might be worth while to place on record the number of animals slaughtered in the last eight years under the act having to do' with tuberculosis. In 1944-45 there were 5,037; in the next year, 3,040 and in the next year 3,659. Then in 1947-48 we put on the larger program, following the war, and the number went up to 12,413. There were 31,106 in the next year; there were 31,426 in the next, and in 1950-51 the figure was 21,019. That is a summary of the total number of animals slaughtered in an effort to eradicate tuberculosis.
How many counties remain to be tested in southern Ontario, or in that part of Ontario known as the older section, as contrasted with the newer section?
The initial test has been completed in all the counties and districts in Ontario.
How many counties now under the accredited area plan have attained that status?

I have here a list somewhat more than a page in length, setting out the

counties in Ontario. I would say there would be 30 or 40 of them.
What would be the percentage, roughly?
I would say about 75 per cent.
I believe quite a few counties were tested only recently for the first time. They could not be accredited areas yet.

According to this list I find 37 of the Ontario counties are accredited, so I was not far out in my estimate. The simple way to get this information would be to secure a copy of this pamphlet. It can be had at any time.
What has been the decrease in the percentage of reactors on second test, as against second-test reactors ten years ago?

In the county of Bruce I find that in 1947 there were 114,029 tested and that 5,324 were reactors. This is a percentage of 4-6. Then in 1930 the percentage in the county of Dundas was 22-4, whereas in 1948 it was only -1 per cent. That gives an indication of what has taken place. The percentage was very heavy in that county 22 years ago. Four years ago, as is seen by the figures, it was down to one-tenth of one per cent. That would seem to be a good illustration of the success in checking the disease.
Prince Edward Island is a disease-free area for cattle. How often must they be tested to maintain their standard?

When the tests show that the number of reactors is reduced to one-half of one per cent the area is accredited for three years, which means that it has to be checked at the end of that time. When it is two-tenths of one per cent it is accredited for six years, at the end of which time the test would be made again. The area is accredited on the basis of the extent to which the disease has been eradicated.

Item agreed to.
25. Compensation for animals slaughtered, including compensation for eggs destroyed from infected premises under terms and conditions approved by the governor in council, $1,040,880.
Has the compensation included in this item anything to do with animals slaughtered by reason of the foot-and-mouth disease?

The amount paid in compensation under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act is in this vote, but the part which

was contributed by reason of the passing of the special act at the beginning of this session was voted in the estimates of last year. It was a special supplementary vote for last year and not this year, and it does not appear in these estimates.

I should like to have a word or two to say on the general foot-and-mouth disease situation. First of all I should like to point out that since the outbreak of the foot-and-mouth disease epidemic or plague members of the Social Credit group have said very little on the floor of the house. There is a definite reason for our reticence.
You are not reticent.

Social Crediters deeply regret the wide and panic-spreading publicity that has been contributed to so substantially by some members of this house. I simply marvel at what they have done. I could name those who have got up on the floor of the house since the outbreak and spread panic-creating propaganda over the world greatly to the detriment of everybody in the Dominion of Canada who is raising stock. I must confess that I simply cannot see how a responsible member of parliament can possibly justify himself in doing that. No Social Crediter contributed in any way, shape or form to any such thing.
On March 3, as recorded at page 43 of Hansard, I said that Social Crediters would expect the government to do everything possible (1) to discover the source of the infection, (2) to determine responsibility, (3) to exterminate the disease and (4) to protect the livestock industry from impairment.
We have been watching the record of the government with respect to these four points. As to the first three, I would say that the government has done very well under the circumstances. It is easy enough to get up and find fault with the performance of any particular group of officers in the field after an incident like the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak has taken place, but I wonder how many of the members who have so voluminously declaimed against the government regarding this matter have computed how many officers it would be necessary to have in the field all across Canada from coast to coast to enable the disease to be detected and more readily and quickly than it was in this instance.
That is the first thing responsible critics ought to take into consideration. I wonder if the men who have had so much to say in criticism and condemnation would be willing to vote the amount of money necessary to pay the increased staff that would
Supply-Agriculture
be needed all over the country to provide the supervision which would be required to detect this kind of outbreak any faster than it was detected. That is the kind of thing Social Crediters have been bearing in mind.
I said a moment ago that I believed the government in the main deserved commendation for the way it had handled the foot-and-mouth disease, that is with respect to the three matters I have mentioned, namely discovering the source of the infection, determining responsibility, and exterminating the disease, which after all were the first things it was necessary to take care of.
As to the fourth point, I believe the federal government has left much to be desired so far as protecting the livestock industry of Canada from serious impairment is concerned. There have been very serious losses. In one of the western newspapers I noticed about four weeks ago an estimate that Alberta had already lost $14 million through decline in livestock prices since the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. That was serious enough, but the amount must be double and probably more than that by now. I have on my desk a pile of over sixty letters from all over my constituency. They are written by farmers who are in the main either feeders of stock or stockmen. These letters serve to indicate the kind of disaster which struck the people of my constituency.
There is a special reason why my constituency was hard hit. As I have pointed out in the house once or twice already, the wet weather last year did a great deal of damage. Many people who had crops in the fields that were snowed under, or that were growing on land too wet to deal with, bought livestock to carry through the year in the hope of having them eat the grain lying on the ground. When the foot-and-mouth disease struck they lost not only what they should have been able to get on the livestock but a great deal of their crop as well. This matter has been given no attention by the government, and probably there are reasons why it would not be; nevertheless that is the kind of situation that has existed in one of the important ridings of this country with respect to the production of grain and livestock.
As I said, I believe the federal government, as regards protecting the livestock industry from impairment, left much to be desired. In the first place I would say the floor prices were altogether too tardily announced. In spite of everything men could do many people became somewhat panicky and began to dispose of their cattle at lower prices than they should have obtained because the floor prices were not announced soon enough. Then

Supp ly-A griculture
when the floor prices were announced they were too low. The lowest floor price which should have been made available to the feeders in my constituency was 28 cents, if they were to be saved from damaging losses. Much of the livestock which were fed in my constituency cost 30 cents in the fall. To offer feeders of such cattle 25 cents for the finished product after they had put into that product their feed and labour was simply to condemn them to heavy losses.
Again, there was the general criticism that the government made no provision for seeing to it that the producers received the full benefit of the floor price. Far too many people reported to me that they simply could not get a price comparable with what the floor price indicated they should be able to get. There were always certain reasons offered by those who would buy, and in many cases producers found it extremely difficult to get people who would buy. There was not adequate provision to see that producers were able to sell their finished animals. The minister will remember the difficulty which arose in 1942 because buyers simply neglected a number of herds by just not coming around or if they did come around-

28.	Grants to fairs and exhibitions, under such terms and conditions as may be approved by the governor in council and subject to allocation by the treasury board, $645,700.

Are there any extra seed fairs in class A now or are they the same as usual? I see there is a reduction in the amount of the grant for these class A fairs. Another question I should like to have answered is, what revenue does the government receive from class A fairs? I understand that the government, through different forms of taxation, secures a greater revenue than the Department of Agriculture pays out in grants.

In answer to the first question, which I understand is whether there are any seed fairs in class A or class B, I may say that there are no seed fairs in those classifications obtaining grants. Exhibits of seed, and that kind of thing, are made at the usual exhibitions.
In answer to the second question, there are no revenues from the class A or B fairs. Our activity in connection with them is the paying of the grants.
There is revenue, but it may not go to the agriculture department. There is revenue from all the betting at the parimutuel machines, and on the tickets that are sold.
There was during wartime. We did get some revenue from that during the war, but it now goes to the provinces.
At page 103 of the details I notice there is an expenditure of $280,000 for building grants. Will the minister indicate the kind of expenditure represented by this item?

Those are agreements-we had one with Brandon-under which we pay

Supply-Agriculture
a part of the cost. It is usually a three-way agreement under which we pay one-third, the province pays one-third and the exhibition board takes care of the other third by some means or other. In some places that portion is met by the municipal corporation in which the exhibition is situated. It is a three-way arrangement under which we pay over a ten-year period.
Would it apply to fairs outside of the A or B classifications?
No, just to A and B.

This is a very important appropriation, $645,700, in which we are directly interested. There is a grant of only $5,500 to the maritime winter fair, which is the senior winter fair in Canada and serves the three maritime provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. It has contributed more over the years to the improvement of livestock in that part of Canada than any other agency. I do not know how long they will be able to continue unless the grant from the federal government is materially increased. The fair could not operate at the present time except for the co-operation of the stock breeders and citizens of the town of Amherst. I gather from this estimate that the same amount is provided this year as was provided last year. I would ask the minister if consideration has not been given to at least doubling the grant to the maritime winter fair. It is urgently needed, and if there is any fair in Canada upon which an expenditure of this kind is warranted it is the maritime winter fair.

The amount, of course, is the same to all fairs right across Canada. The general grant is $5,000. I note that Amherst does earn another $500. The extra $500 is for junior work, but I presume if the others did the same work they could earn the $500. It is just a general grant of that amount for each fair, and it is not expected we are going to increase it.
I want to point out to the minister and the committee that with present-day costs the grant is inadequate. There should be a minimum of $10,000.

Can the minister tell us whose responsibility it is to classify the fairs? Has there been any change this year? I understand that one or two of their fairs in my own district have asked for reclassification. Have there been any changes in those classifications this year, and how many have increased their classifications?

Whether it is a class A or B fair is determined in the first instance by provincial classification. In so far as we are

concerned, we pay a grant provided the fair has paid out a certain amount in prizes for three years. If application is made after qualifying in that way, consideration is then given to the application.
What are the different classifications, other than A and B?

Has Paris been reclassified this year?
No, Paris has not.
Both Paris and Rockton have asked for reclassification. Has Rockton fair been reclassified?
Rockton is under investigation now, and so is Paris, but neither of them is in.
Neither has been accepted yet?
No.

I understand it is made just as soon as we get the evidence in and the facts are established. I understand that evidence has come in very recently, but the decision has not yet been announced.
It has been in quite a while.
I cannot tell you when it came in, but apparently it is in.

Marketing service-
30.	Marketing service administration, $259,498.
Mr. Cold well: Can the minister give us a brief resume of just exactly what is involved in these marketing services and what cooperation there is between this branch and the Department of Trade and Commerce? The two departments are engaged in marketing. I notice that the main amounts in this particular appropriation of $216,265 out of the $259,498 are for salaries. Perhaps the minister could give us briefly a summary of the work of this branch. I am not asking for a long explanation, but just for a few words.

Having regard to general agricultural products, the two branches are concerned with the home market and the market outside of Canada. That is, we have charge of the marketing of all farm products in Canada with the exception of grain.
Within the country?
Within the country.
That is what I thought.

All activities in connection with that matter are carried on by us. But when it comes to the matter of advertising outside of Canada or to carrying on activities in connection with the marketing of a product, that is something which is carried on through the Department of Trade and Commerce. We have a few men in Britain. We have one man established in London. Then we have, I think, six inspectors under him at the different ports. We take care of that part of the marketing cost.
I think probably the point that is in the mind of the hon. member has to do with the different methods by which the grading and all the administration activities having to do with the marketing of grain are carried on. That is charged up to the grain. It is carried on through the Department of Trade and Commerce, the head office being at Winnipeg. The reason for that is largely the fact that in the beginning it had to do altogether with wheat and has been applied more or less to oats and barley since we put oats and barley under the wheat board. It had to do with wheat because practically all the wheat that was grown in Canada and that was being shipped long distances passed through Winnipeg. It was therefore a simple matter to have all the inspection and the grading done there at Winnipeg.
That procedure could not be made to apply to other farm products. For example, with regard to cattle, there are probably as many marketed at Toronto or at Montreal as at any other point. Some are marketed at Calgary, Edmonton and so on. You cannot take any one point and set up an organization 55704-245J
Supply-Agriculture
there on the basis that any of the other products would pass through there. We take care of the inspection, grading and all activities having to do with the marketing of those products. That activity is paid for out of these votes. There is that difference between the grading of grain and the grading of the other products. The cost of carrying on that marketing activity is charged up to the treasury of Canada; but as to grain, it is charged up to the farmer's grain and is paid for out of that. That is the main difference between the two.

The reason I had for asking the questions was that today I sent to the Minister of Trade and Commerce the original of a letter that I had from Britain. I do not know why I was written to about it. The letter reads as follows:
For many years prior to the war we imported thousands of Canadian turkeys.
Since the war, we have made many but so far unsuccessful attempts to recommence this trading, due chiefly to the dollar situation.
If possible, we would like to have a supply for Christmas of 1952 and would be obliged to hear if you can possibly help us.
Our approximate requirements are 10,000 hen turkeys 8 lbs. to 12 lbs. each.
The enclosed letter will substantiate our remarks.
The enclosed letter which I also forwarded to the Minister of Trade and Commerce simply indicates that this was a bona fide dealer who has dealt extensively in Canada in years gone by. I presume the difficulty arose through the dollar situation. I was wondering what facilities there might be, either through the minister's marketing agency or through the Department of Trade and Commerce, to try to open up a market of that description for poultry, turkeys in particular which may this year, as they were in the United States two years ago, be in over-supply. I have always thought some arrangement might be made, and I offered a suggestion in connection with the $1,200,000,000 British loan, that payments might be deferred without interest if the amounts coming to Canada, last year about $26 million, were used within this country for the purchase of farm products like cheese, apples, poultry and so on. I sent the letter to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as I said. I suppose I sent it to the right minister. Is any part of the minister's organization engaged in this activity, namely in trying to find ways and means of disposing of poultry, for example, and meeting the requirements of dealers like this Mr. John Donaldson who wrote to me from Manchester, England, under date of June 6 of this year?

There is, of necessity, close co-operation between the Department of

Supply-Agriculture
Trade and Commerce and this department. They get their information from us as to what the surplus of a product is likely to be. If there is no surplus of the product to be sold outside this country, of course the Department of Trade and Commerce would not have any considerable interest in it; and probably we would not be required to have much interest in it either, other than to keep check on it, because the trade itself would fairly well take care of any transactions in it.
With regard to a surplus to sell anywhere, immediately we get information which indicates that there is a great surplus, as we have this year in connection with the production of turkeys, we make a search for markets. Unfortunately for us there is a great increase in the United States as well. The two increases may make it rather difficult for us to market as many as we would desire to market in the United States. But when it comes to marketing in Britain, of course the problem with regard to turkeys is the same as it is with regard to anything else, namely that Britain is more likely to buy her supply from sterling areas, if she can get it, than she is to buy it here. If she were going to buy it here, I am afraid the price would not be anything like what we would expect in this country. But in any case we search for markets wherever we can find them.

I think probably I can say what a moment ago I intended to say, under this item, because it has to do with marketing. May I just preface the brief remarks which I shall make tonight upon this matter by reading an excerpt from the minister's speech before the Canadian Club at Winnipeg on January 9, 1952. He used these words, which I think have great significance:
My conversations convinced me that Britain's need for our food is as great as ever. We are supplying her with more wheat and flour than ever before in pre-war peacetime. We are supplying her with less of every other food we produce than at any other time over a long period. We should be able to find some way of making a trade with Britain and others which will result in our being able to send our food in exchange for something she has which we want.
That which she has, which we need more than any other thing, is people. Sir Clifford Sifton stated at one time that each immigrant was worth $1,000 to Canada. I am sure we will all agree now, fifty years later, that he was right. If an immigrant was worth $1,000 in his day, one is worth $2,500 today; 100,000 immigrants would be worth $250 million.
That figure could be multiplied to whatever multiple is necessary by moving surplus population from Britain to Canada. They would produce raw materials and food here to help keep employed and feed those at home. If that kind of an ex-

change cannot be satisfactorily worked out to balance over 50 years, it is not dollars that are lacking, it is ideas.
I should like to concentrate for a minute or two on "the ideas". How in the name of common sense is it that we cannot find in the government "ideas" which are necessary to enable the minister to transact the negotiations which he visualized on that occasion? When I was talking about the effect of foot-and-mouth disease on the people in my constituency, great numbers of whom are stock producers-
Louder, please.
Can't you keep your peace at all?
Are you looking at me?
Whoever made the remark.
Don't look at me.

In my constituency the feeders were very seriously injured because there was no adequate means of taking off the surplus products that became ready for market. A similar problem is beginning to face us in Canadian agriculture, as we might say, all across the board. If we cannot now solve the problem of selling turkeys, for example, which was the question the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar raised, to Britain when the British need the turkeys and we need the market for the turkeys, then it is high time we concentrated all our energies for a while on the solution of that problem. It is obviously a problem that depends on money, it is a problem that ought to be possible of solution.
I would say to the minister that my main criticism of his handling of the stock situation in connection with the foot-and-mouth disease is this: As soon as the outbreak occurred the minister should have declared that the government would buy all the surplus beef, pork and mutton as it became ready for the market. The government would not have had to buy directly from the producers; they could have bought from the packing plants enough to make room for the products that became ready for markets. They could then have sent those meat surpluses to Britain as a gift.
The question would be raised immediately, where would we get the money? Well, first of all would that have been the solution? Certainly that would have been the solution. If the government had announced that it would take the surplus just as fast as it became ready for the market, just as though that surplus were going to the United States, and sent the surpluses to Britain on a line

of interest-free credit, even then there would have been no tragic fall in prices such as was registered all across Canada, with consequent losses immeasurable and incalculable to the livestock industry of Canada and the Canadian economy generally.
The question will be raised as to whether or not the money could have been found. I do not intend to go into details. I referred to this matter yesterday in a talk on the finance bill. I want to refer to what happened in world war I for the minister's sake. I think he was right in the chamber when I was mentioning it. In world war I the Canadian government created money under the Finance Act of 1914 and bought $50 million worth of wheat and passed it to Britain. They received no return for some time. By 1927 Britain had paid back all of the loan with goods which Canada had accepted from Britain, but the important things to bear in mind in this connection are these: That money did not cost Canadians a cent. It was not borrowed from anyone; it was not taxed from anyone. It was good money. It bought the wheat; it paid the men who produced the wheat. It was just as valuable to the Canadian economy as any money that possibly could have been put into the Canadian economy, and it would have been valuable and continued valuable even if Britain had never repaid with goods. Once we can register that simple fact, and the minister can get it accepted by a sufficient number of the cabinet, starting with the Minister of Finance, then we will have the "ideas" with which to solve that problem which he propounded before that important audience in January, 1952; until he can find a solution such as that there is no solution available. Knowing the simple fact, he could have dealt, and now would be able to deal, with the problem of marketing our surpluses.
Let us all face that fact. Either we strangle our agriculture to death at this time, when we are capable of the greatest production in our history, and when the world needs that production more than it ever did in all history-either we strangle our agriculture to death and cease to play as important a part in world affairs, and cease to keep our economy prosperous, or we find the "ideas" with which to market abroad without having goods coming in from foreign countries.
That illustration I have given, and which I gave yesterday, shows what can be done. I think I can safely encourage the minister to defy any member of the cabinet, or all of them put together, to show why that simple device would not have worked in the case of the foot-and-mouth disease. It would have
Supply-Agriculture
saved Canadian stock producers great quantities of money; saved them from disposing of their livestock, their breeding stock, and saved them from losing confidence in the future, with all the evil effects that are going to devolve from those three ill results.
If one bears in mind that this device could have been used, then I think he must realize that the Department of Agriculture and the Canadian government were open to severe censure in their method of dealing with the marketing situation which developed from the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. Therefore that is the criticism I have to offer, and the reason I offer it. And that is the suggestion I have for the future.

Item agreed to.
31.	Agricultural economics, $579,455.
What is the function of these various economists who are listed on page 105 under this item of $579,000? What functions do they perform?

These are the men who operate under Dr. Booth, the chief economist of the department. They make investigations with regard to cost of production across the country, and investigations with regard to marketing. These investigations are going on constantly in different parts of the country.

Do they do any work to determine what might be an economic unit in various types of farming, say in the dairy industry; whether ten head of milk cows or twenty head of milk cows would make an economic unit on a farm, or how many acres of orchard may be an economic unit, or how many acres under cultivation in grain in western Canada? Is any work done by that department to ascertain this information?
They conduct surveys in co-operation with the provinces on all matters of that kind, and they do make reports on units which may help in different kinds of production.
Are any available that have been made in recent years?
Yes; they are being published constantly, and can be obtained.
Under what item does the minister want us to ask questions regarding products purchased under the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
Under item 51.

I want to make it quite clear that it is not just the administration of the Agricultural Prices Support Act that I want to ask about. I want to make sure I will not be out of order when I get down to item 51.

Supply-Agriculture
The amount of money available is in the supplementaries. It could be discussed under that item.
What publicity is given to these reports of economic units, or other work done by this group?
They are listed monthly in a publication that is put out by the department, and can be obtained by writing to the information service.
Are many published? When a booklet of this description is published, how many are available?

Different numbers are published, depending upon whether they are simply published for the use of experts, or whether they are to be distributed to different groups. If they are for general distribution many more of them are published. It would depend upon what experience has shown would be a proper distribution.

My hon. friend and I are interested in seeing that the reports are made available. Here is a group of men who are not only capable but who are important to the industry. These economists perform a most useful service. How are people encouraged to get their reports and make the best use of them? If I were to be given a list of publications it might mean something or it might mean very little. Are they reviewed in any way, so that anyone looking at the list would realize the importance of certain of these documents?

I have known Dr. Booth over the years. He began his activities on a farm in Saskatchewan. I believe he was the first economist employed, years ago, by a provincial government. He has been a fairly good publicist himself. He has always seen to it that, in respect of any of these that are important, a review is given to the press. These reviews of course induce many to write for the publications. The only means, however, by which individuals can find out what these publications are is to send in to our publicity branch for a list of all the publications in the department. This will be sent to anyone asking for it, free of charge. These particular publications are also free to anyone asking for them.

It is about the same as last year. I understand the grade A's are about 32 per cent.
What has happened in the last three months would have knocked that figure out of balance.
Grades A and B together are about 75 per cent.
But there nas been a considerable change in the last three months. What effect has it had on the variation of grades?
I understand there has not been much change. However, we will have the information tomorrow.
Has the department increased the allowance for lime for the farmers of Nova Scotia during the past year?
As I said a moment ago, this operation is carried on by the province. We contribute 60 per cent of the cost.
If a farmer pays an additional amount, does that revert to the federal government?
No; we receive no money back.

speechtext: Tomorrow we will consider the Senate amendments to Bill No. 306, to amend the Combines Investigation Act. I understand the government has no objection to these amendments which are coming from the other place, so they will take no time. Then we will consider Bill No. 393, to readjust the representation of the House of Commons. That may take a little more time. Then we will take the balance of the estimates, agriculture, post office, national revenue, legislation, citizenship and immigration, finance and any other remaining items.
May I ask the leader whether the house will sit after six o'clock tomorrow night?
